articles.title: Russian retribution, Islamic NATO, showdown in the West Bank, the German spy machine: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
Russian retribution, Islamic NATO, showdown in the West Bank, the German spy machine: RT stories that shaped the week
Once the naked hatred of German journalism prompted Vladimir Zelensky’s most fervent British backers to criticize Ukraine’s “gamification of killing” Russians, things went from bad to worse for Kiev – on the battlefield and in the diplomatic arena.
Russia punishes Ukraine with ‘harsher methods’
Vladimir Zelensky’s long-range strikes against Russia have already provoked a fearsome response from Moscow, but the Ukrainian leader doubled down this week, with his forces killing more than a dozen civilians in drone raids on Tatarstan and Krasnodar.
Russia responded by wiping out military-industrial and dual-use facilities in Kiev and Zaporozhye and destroying port infrastructure on Ukraine’s Black Sea coast. RT has already covered Russia’s campaign against Ukrainian ports in detail, which Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said will intensify in an interview released on Friday morning.
“We will not sink to their level,” he told the Russian media, referring to Ukraine’s targeting of civilians. “Instead, we will adopt much harsher methods to destroy everything that enables the West to fuel Kiev’s war machine. We are already doing this, and they are already moaning.”
Zelensky’s moaning, as Lavrov calls it, has been directed at his Western donors, who possess a dwindling supply of Patriot interceptor missiles that could help repel Russia’s missile barrages. However, the US used the bulk of the world’s Patriots in its war on Iran, and the Europeans aren’t in the mood to share. Moreover, as RT explained, Zelensky’s math is fundamentally flawed. Even if he were to get all the missiles he wanted, he’d only have enough interceptors to repel two attacks at best.
With all other options exhausted, Ukraine reportedly asked Russia for a truce with regard to attacks on shipping in the Black Sea. Moscow rejected the proposal, with Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accusing Kiev of “brazen acts of terrorism” against civilian ships and ruling out “half-measures that merely grant the Kiev regime a temporary breathing space.”
Zelensky learns how to lose friends and influence
At a time when Ukraine needs all the help it can get, Zelensky seemingly went out of his way to further irritate one of his most important backers. Poland is one of only three European countries that have given Patriot missiles to Ukraine this year. This week Kiev repaid Warsaw’s generosity by exhuming the remains of Nazi collaborator Evgeny Konovalets – who gave the Third Reich intelligence used to carry out the mass murder of Poles – from a grave in Rotterdam, while announcing he would be buried with full military honors in Ukraine.
Diplomatic relations between Poland and Ukraine are already strained due to Kiev’s stubborn veneration of Nazi collaborators, and the Polish public’s goodwill toward Ukraine is evaporating. According to a poll published on Wednesday, 67% of Poles support the deportation of unemployed Ukrainian men living in Poland as refugees.
Across the Atlantic, US Vice President JD Vance reportedly gave Zelensky a dressing down for attacking Black Sea shipping. According to the Financial Times, Vance’s patience reached its limit when Ukrainian forces attacked ships bound for a partly US-owned terminal in Russia’s port of Novorossiysk.
Russia frees US Marine
Diplomacy paid off for the US this week when Russia agreed to release former US Marine Robert Gilman, who was arrested in 2022 after a drunken assault on a policeman in Russia. Gilman was pardoned by Russian President Vladimir Putin and arrived back on US soil on Tuesday.
Welcome home, Robert Gilman! 🇺🇸
After more than four years detained in Russia, American citizen Robert Gilman is finally back on U.S. soil.
Thanks to the Trump Admin, another American is safely home where he belongs.
God bless Robert Gilman, and GOD BLESS AMERICA. 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/Tn8C8h9QBD
“After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a humanitarian basis,” US President Donald Trump stated. “We appreciate this decision.” US envoy Steve Witkoff apparently played a central role in the negotiations and thanked Putin for his “personal engagement throughout this process.”
Gilman’s mental health has reportedly deteriorated in incarceration, and he is expected to receive treatment at home in Texas.
Germany’s spy expansion
Thousands of Germans protested in the eastern German state of Saxony this week, demanding lower energy costs, tougher migration policies, and an end to reckless military spending. What Chancellor Merz’s government offered instead was a suite of new powers for the country’s foreign and domestic intelligence agencies, the BND and BfV respectively.
Under the new legislation tabled by Merz’s Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, the BND will be permitted to carry out offensive cyberattacks on Russia and other foreign adversaries, while the BfV will be allowed to infiltrate Germans’ smartphones and computers. The new powers were described as “a revolution” by Dobrindt. Moscow described them as another example of Germany’s “rabid militarization,” while Germany’s right-wing AfD warned that they will turn the BfV “from an early warning system of democracy into an architect of a totalitarian reality.” We’ve seen this before in Germany, and it did not end well.
The BfV’s new powers will likely be turned against the AfD, the country’s most popular political party and a poll-topper in Saxony. The agency has already tried to list the party as a “right-wing extremist” group and been granted permission to surveil the AfD’s Bavaria chapter.
The rise of Islamic NATO
As Europe tears itself apart, the Middle East’s Sunni powers are drawing closer together – with profound implications for the region. Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan signed the ‘Mecca Pact’ this week, agreeing to treat an attack against one member as an attack against all three. However, it remains unclear how the three countries would react to such an attack. The so-called ‘Islamic NATO’ has already been criticised in Iran as a “paper agreement” that will make Saudi Arabia no safer than the presence of American troops on its soil.
In Moscow, experts at the Middle East Studies Center analyzed the pact and broke down its implications. Writing exclusively for RT, the center’s president, Murad Sadygzade, explained how its members will have the task of deterring both Israel and Iran – all without overt US involvement. The center’s vice-president, Mishel Bychkova, views the pact in narrower terms: as an opportunity for Türkiye to leverage its massive defense industry and consolidate its growing power in the region.
If any country is concerned about the pact, it’s India, foreign policy analyst Robinder Nath Sachdev told RT India on Tuesday. With a nuclear-armed Pakistan strengthening its alliances, New Delhi must work out what it needs to do “to counter this new reality, which is a worrisome reality,” he said. He added that India will have to look at “our other partnerships with other nations, including, of course, Russia.”
Tucker meets RT
As the fallout from Tucker Carlson’s political manifesto continues to settle, historian and RT columnist Tarik Cyril Amar looked at why Israel is potentially more worried about a third-party challenge by Carlson than the US Republican establishment is. Meanwhile, RT’s Rick Sanchez sat down with Carlson himself for an exclusive, hour-long interview.
Carlson ruled out any plans to run for president, but unloaded on the US’ “criminal” leadership class, the “permanent bureaucracy,” and the Democrat/Republican consensus on money and foreign policy that has created a “one-party state posing as a democracy.” The conservative journalist revealed how Israel had attempted to recruit him to share the infamous Hunter Biden laptop story in 2020, and promised to keep speaking out against the neocon “war lobby” and Israeli influence in Washington, no matter the risk.
“What are you going to do about it? Kill me? OK, I’m not afraid of that. I’m a Christian. So I’m just going to keep talking,” he told Sanchez in one particularly powerful exchange.
Showdown in the West Bank
The US-Israeli alliance seemed to meet its limits this week when a group of armed Israeli settlers laid siege to three Palestinian families in their homes in the West Bank village of Qusra. As it turns out, one of these families had relatives living in the US, and the response from Washington was unusually sharp.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee – who has previously equated Tucker Carlson’s criticism of Israel with antisemitism – described the settlers as “unsettlers” and “Israeli terrorists,” saying that “doing this to this family’s home is criminal.” Huckabee is typically supportive of the illegal settlement of Palestinian land, and his condemnation of this incident looked like an attempt to draw a line between ‘good’ and ‘bad’ settlers as much as a message to West Jerusalem.

articles.title: Meltdowns and meager meals: How bad is the situation aboard US aircraft carrier attacking Iran?
articles.body:
Meltdowns and meager meals: How bad is the situation aboard US aircraft carrier attacking Iran?
The USS Abraham Lincoln has been grappling with dismal conditions for months during the US-Israeli war on Iran, amid mounting reports of severe exhaustion, supply shortages, and mental-health problems among crew members. The problems have sparked an uproar among crew members’ families and prompted demands for answers from US lawmakers.
The vessel, a 5,000-person nuclear-powered Nimitz-class aircraft carrier capable of carrying up to 90 aircraft and conducting more than 100 combat sorties a day at peak capacity, left San Diego in late November. It has now been deployed for more than 260 days, including more than 200 consecutive days at sea – an extraordinary stretch by Navy standards.
On top of that, the flattop has spent much of that time in a combat environment, with Iran claiming to have targeted it on numerous occasions. Even as US officials insist the carrier remains operational, the hardships of a prolonged campaign appear to be taking their toll.
Here is what we know about the issues facing the aircraft carrier and its crew.
What are conditions like aboard the Abraham Lincoln?
The complaints from crew members and their families go well beyond the usual discomforts of a long deployment.
They include shortages of toothpaste, deodorant, and soap, problems with hot and potable water, broken toilets, unreliable laundry facilities, disruptions to food supplies, and mail delays so severe that some care packages reportedly disappeared into the system for months. Other reports describe mold, failing plumbing, and holes worn through parts of the flight deck from extensive use without adequate repairs.
Democratic Congressman Mike Levin claimed that the food situation is so bad that crew members’ meals “came down to half a cup of rice and two tortillas.” The meager meals were first reported by USA Today as early as mid-April, although the Pentagon denied that there were food shortages at the time.
The USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea for more than 250 days, pushing its crew to the limit. Sailors report exhaustion, deteriorating living conditions, shortages of basic supplies and serious food problems: small portions, poor-quality meals and periods of depleted stocks. The… https://t.co/iWYaeKchzUpic.twitter.com/C4cheR4N2M
— Tom Antonov (@Tom_Antonov) August 13, 2026
According to Maritime Executive, the supply problems are partly due to logistics, as the main base of the 5th Fleet is located in Bahrain, deep inside the Persian Gulf, meaning many shipments must pass through the Strait of Hormuz and risk Iranian strikes.
Is the crew burning out?
There are strong indications that it is. One of the most striking episodes confirmed by CENTCOM occurred on August 3, when a sailor went overboard from the Abraham Lincoln and was recovered roughly an hour later.
🚨🇮🇷🇺🇸 Text messages from a sailor aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln reveal no milk in three months and ROTTEN food arriving at sea...
He reportedly wrote that almost nothing fresh makes it out except meat, because only frozen goods survive the supply run, and called it the worst… pic.twitter.com/ylCgsHap26
Citing US officials, CNN reported that the Navy treated the incident as a mental-health episode, adding that the sailor was medically evaluated and later removed from the ship for further care.
Annabelle Loma, the serviceman’s wife, told Navy Times that her husband had become emotionally exhausted and confirmed that he had attempted to take his own life by jumping overboard. She added that he seemed “scared” and was afraid he would receive “a dishonorable discharge, and just because he was burnt out.”
At a meeting with Navy leaders, another spouse said her husband had sent a message saying he hoped he “doesn’t wake up tomorrow,” according to Stars and Stripes.
Other families have also sounded the alarm over the physical and mental exhaustion after months of long shifts, warning that such levels of fatigue could lead to deadly mistakes.
“The morale is not good,” one family member said, as cited by MS Now. “Apparently, the ship’s doctor or therapist said they need to hit port soon, or people are going to start, you know, losing their minds.”
The Navy, however, has pushed back against such concerns, telling CNN that “we have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship.”
Could stress on the flattop lead to violence?
Citing an unnamed “informed military source,” Iranian news agency Tasnim reported earlier this month that seven US Navy personnel had been killed and several others wounded in a violent confrontation aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.
According to the report, an adviser to CENTCOM, commander Adm. Brad Cooper, boarded the carrier to address complaints about the prolonged deployment but was booed and pelted with water bottles before the confrontation escalated into a knife fight.
CENTCOM denied the allegation, saying that no crew members aboard the carrier had died during the Iran war.
How much pressure has Iran put on the Abraham Lincoln?
Multiple analyses have suggested that Iran, which is militarily inferior to the US, has been relying on attritional warfare to hold its ground and gain concessions from Washington. Kamal Kharrazi, head of Iran’s Strategic Council on Foreign Relations, said Iran was prepared for a “long war” and argued that the longer the conflict continued, the greater the economic pressure on other countries would become.
Maj. Gen. Mohammad Jafar Asadi, a former senior commander, described the conflict in July as an “attritional and never-ending war.”
As the conflict has dragged on, Tehran has claimed to have mounted numerous attacks on the Abraham Lincoln. On March 1, Iran announced it had fired four ballistic missiles at the carrier, with CENTCOM saying the missiles “didn’t even come close.” Later that month, Tehran claimed that missiles and drones had struck the vessel, rendering it inoperable and forcing it to withdraw – an allegation also rejected by Washington.
In early April, Iran said it had launched multiple waves of attack drones toward the Abraham Lincoln group in the northern Indian Ocean, forcing it to withdraw.
In July, it claimed to have struck logistics support centers serving US aircraft carriers in Oman, later adding that other targets included “one aircraft carrier refueling platform,” alongside fuel depots, naval stores, aircraft facilities, and other US military infrastructure. On Tuesday, the Iranian military claimed that the US had no warships left in the Persian Gulf region.
While it is unclear whether the Abraham Lincoln sustained any damage during the attacks, it was hardly operating in a benign environment, with CENTCOM reporting roughly 10,000 aircraft flights and the expenditure of about 1.5 million pounds of ordnance during the mission.
What beef do US lawmakers have with the Pentagon?
On Wednesday, a member of the US Senate’s Armed Services Committee, Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, published an open letter to Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, raising “serious concerns” about the situation aboard the ship and questioning whether it could sustain continued operations.
“The Lincoln is not an isolated case. Recent carrier deployments have repeatedly stretched beyond their originally anticipated durations, suggesting that extended deployments may be becoming a feature rather than an exception of the Navy’s force-generation model,” he added.
Fellow Senator Ruben Gallego has called for a bipartisan congressional oversight visit to the Abraham Lincoln, casting doubt on Pentagon assurances.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer has gone further, blaming Hegseth personally and saying sailors are “paying the price” for Pentagon failures. “When Pete Hegseth was nominated, everyone knew he was completely incompetent... Pete Hegseth must be fired immediately,” he insisted.
What does the Pentagon say in response to the accusations?
Hegseth dismissed reports of poor living conditions and food shortages aboard the Abraham Lincoln as “completely misrepresented,” while acknowledging that some deployments could last longer and be tougher than others.
“We make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain, has everything that we can provide them at every single moment,” he added.
Meanwhile, the AP reported that the USS George Washington is now moving toward the Middle East from Vietnam to replace the Abraham Lincoln. The redeployment is expected to weaken the US footprint in the Pacific amid tensions with China, however.
Bottom Line
While the Pentagon insists that the Abraham Lincoln “remains fully capable of meeting all mission tasking,” and there is no credible evidence that Iran managed to cripple the ship, its crew appears to have come dangerously close to the breaking point.
After more than eight months of deployment, the vessel appears to be struggling with logistics and supplies of basic amenities, amid growing concerns over its crew members’ mental health. While the Abraham Lincoln is expected to be relieved soon, its performance raises questions about Washington’s overall ability to sustain effective long-term operations against even a militarily inferior adversary.

articles.body:
US President Donald Trump stated on Friday, Aug. 14, that he intends to declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory following the conclusion of the war with Iran.
Accoding to Clash Report, speaking at the David S. Mack Training and Intelligence Center in Garden City, Trump said the US currently controls the waterway.

Reuters reported that commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz nearly halted on Friday following attacks on two additional vessels. The US government indicated it is prepared to maintain the maritime blockade indefinitely.
A senior Iranian source stated that negotiations to extend a June ceasefire agreement yielded no results. Following the breakdown of the ceasefire, Iran resumed attacks on vessels it claims are attempting to navigate the strait without authorization from Tehran.
Trump on Iran:
Pretty soon, I will be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States. pic.twitter.com/ySyIIhvF5V
Iranian demands and prior negotiations
The escalation follows a list of demands issued by Iran for reopening the strait.
Mohammad Bagher Zolqadr, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, stated that Tehran requires the immediate lifting of the US naval blockade, the withdrawal of US military forces, an end to hostilities, financial compensation, and access to frozen assets.
Zelensky Struggles to Find Ukraine’s Next Envoy to Trump
On Aug. 2, Trump announced a temporary suspension of planned US military strikes to allow for diplomatic negotiations. He stipulated the immediate opening of the strait as a primary condition for any agreement.
Impact on US weapons stockpiles
The ongoing conflict has resulted in a depletion of US military stockpiles, affecting security commitments in other regions. The US has utilized over 1,500 Patriot interceptor missiles in the Middle East, reducing its current inventory to fewer than 1,700 units.
The shortage of Patriot systems, along with ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles, has delayed arms shipments to partners in Europe and Asia, affecting Ukraine’s air defense capabilities against Russian attacks. In the Indo-Pacific, the Pentagon redeployed air defense units, naval destroyers, and Tomahawk missiles from allied nations to support the Middle East campaign.
In response, the US Department of Defense directed defense contractors to accelerate production. Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg issued a letter to leading defense companies requiring plans within 21 days to expand manufacturing capacity for critical weapons.

articles.title: US military loses 25% of its MQ-9 drones as stocks dwindle in Iran war
articles.body:
US military loses 25% of its MQ-9 drones as stocks dwindle in Iran war
TEHRAN — The US military has suffered a 25% reduction in its MQ-9 Reaper drone fleet during the conflict with Iran, losing at least 45 aircraft valued at over $1.3 billion combined.
The Reaper can cost between $30 million and $50 million depending on the type of sensors and weapons it carries, according to the Air Force.
Heavy operations over the vital Strait of Hormuz—coupled with enemy strikes and persistent communications failures—have severely depleted these high-value surveillance and strike platforms alongside critical missile stockpiles, leaving US inventory stretched thin and forcing major strategic adjustments across the region.
The mounting drone losses reflect a broader, systemic strain on American military readiness as the campaign drags on. Before the outbreak of hostilities on February 28, the US military maintained a fleet of approximately 185 Reapers across the Air Force and Marine Corps, excluding classified intelligence assets. By May, senior Air Force leadership confirmed to Congress that active inventory had dropped to around 135 units. While the Marine Corps’ Pacific-based Reapers have avoided losses, the Air Force fleet patrolling Middle Eastern airspace has taken the brunt of the attrition. Flying at slow speeds and relatively low altitudes, the non-stealthy aircraft have proven to be vulnerable targets for Iranian forces and resistance groups operating in Yemen and Iraq.
Beyond uncrewed aircraft, the sheer intensity of the air campaign has rapidly drained America’s most advanced munitions. In the first month of hostilities alone, US forces expended over 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles and more than 1,000 Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors. This unprecedented burn rate—compounded by years of prior military assistance to Ukraine—has severely degraded stockpiles of key long-range strike capabilities and high-demand air defenses. Consequently, frontline commanders have been forced to change defensive tactics, rationing interceptors and holding back missiles in reserve unless an incoming strike poses a direct threat to personnel or key installations.
Restocking these depleted arsenals presents a daunting long-term industrial challenge. While the White House is pressing Congress for a $67 billion emergency supplemental war budget, financial infusions alone cannot overcome manufacturing bottlenecks. Analysis from defense think tanks highlights that critical systems face multi-year production backlogs. For instance, manufacturing a single THAAD interceptor takes nearly three years, with maximum national production capacity capped at just 96 units annually. Meeting the Pentagon’s multi-year requirement for thousands of interceptors could take decades at current factory output levels.

articles.title: Ukrainian Defense Firm DEMZ to Build Ammunition Plant in Lithuania
articles.body:
Lithuania’s Ministry of Economy and Innovation has signed an agreement with the Ukrainian defense company DEMZ to establish an ammunition manufacturing plant in the country, Delfi reported
The project involves operations in two locations. A new manufacturing facility will be built in the Prienai district, while production will also take place at an existing site in Alytus.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Construction of the new facility is scheduled to begin in autumn 2026, with production expected to launch by the end of 2027.
The plant will manufacture ammunition meeting NATO standards. The production will initially supply the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU), with plans to eventually export to allied nations.
The project incorporates research and development initiatives for new technological solutions. DEMZ also stated plans to recruit workers of varying skill levels and implement specialized professional training programs.
Defense cooperation framework
The ammunition plant agreement follows a bilateral defense cooperation pact signed by Ukraine and Lithuania in May.
That agreement focuses on expanding joint production, technology transfer, and defense manufacturing between companies from both nations.
The framework prioritizes the development of unmanned platforms, advanced drone technologies, and air and missile defense systems.
The agreement also includes provisions for Ukrainian military experts to assist in developing modern security capabilities in Lithuania.
Ukraine Condemns Russian Move to Erase Borders With Occupied Areas
Regional security context
Lithuania, which shares borders with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Belarus, has tripled its defense spending since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In July, Lithuanian lawmakers initiated the process of lifting a constitutional ban on stationing nuclear weapons on the country’s territory.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda stated the change was necessary due to deteriorating geopolitical circumstances, though he noted there were no immediate plans to store nuclear weapons in Lithuania.
Lithuanian officials have cited regional security risks, including mobilization efforts and intensified combat training announced by Belarus, as factors necessitating enhanced defense coordination.

articles.title: Ukraine says it has struck Russian 'rocket and space' centre
articles.body:
Additional strikes were carried out on Savasleyka air base - which Ukraine said housed aircraft used for missile attacks - and an oil facility in Ust-Luga, per Zelenskyy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Saturday that Ukrainian forces had struck the Progress Rocket and Space Centre in Russia's Samara region, a facility involved in the manufacturing and operation of space launch vehicles.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy said Ukraine hit the centre with FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, describing it as one of Russian space agency Roscosmos' "key enterprises" and saying it was involved in "electronics production".
Additional strikes were carried out on Savasleyka air base in the Nizhny Novgorod region - which the Ukrainian leader said housed aircraft used for missile attacks on Ukraine - and an oil facility in Ust-Luga, close to the border with Estonia, per Zelenskyy.
He shared video footage on X appearing to show the aftermath of some of the strikes. Large columns of black smoke and flames can be seen at sites in the distance.
"Our plan of long-range sanctions against Russia for this war is being implemented, and it is important that Russia’s war potential be reduced," Zelenskyy wrote.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has since shared more details on the operation as well as its intelligence on the targets, confirming hits were recorded at both the Progress centre and the air base and that a fire had broken out on the facilities' grounds.
It added that the launch vehicles produced at the Progress centre were used to "place Russian military, reconnaissance, and communications spacecraft into orbit."
The Savasleyka air base, the General Staff added, is used to operate MiG-31K fighter jets, which it said were used to carry Kh-47M2 Kinzhal ballistic missiles.
Ukraine's 'long-range sanctions' and Russian strikes
Ukraine has repeatedly hit targets deep inside Russia in an effort to increase pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin and the country's military capabilities and to squeeze the Russian economy.
Kyiv has in particular sought to home in on energy facilities across Russia as part of this strategy, striking oil refineries, terminals, and depots across the country. The attacks have led to fuel shortages across parts of Russia and Russian-occupied territories.
The Ukrainian air force said on Saturday that Russian forces had launched 152 drones and loitering munitions at Ukraine overnight.
"According to preliminary data, as of 9 am, air defences had shot down or neutralised 124 enemy UAVs," it said, adding that strikes had been recorded in 16 locations.
Russian attacks on the Kherson region in southern Ukraine over the past day injured 28 people, including a child, according to Oleksandr Prokudin, the head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration.
A child was also killed and 11 people were injured in a series of strikes on the Dnipropetrovsk region in southeast Ukraine, per regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha, while four were injured in Sumy Oblast in the country's north.
A further nine people were injured across the regions of Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kharkiv, per local authorities.

articles.title: Why Tehran Fears President Zelensky
articles.body:
Iran’s rulers call Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky a “clown,” a Western puppet, and the leader of a criminal gang. Yet the intensity of their response suggests something different.
After a Ukrainian strike in the Caspian Sea hit an Iranian commercial vessel, regime officials and media outlets issued threats and debated retaliation. Some urged Tehran to punish European governments supporting Kyiv. For a leader they claim to dismiss, President Zelensky commands a remarkable amount of the Islamic Republic’s attention.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Tehran’s concern is not President Zelensky’s rhetoric. It is Ukraine’s ability to impose costs on the military partnership between the regime and Russia.
The regime supplied Russia with Shahed drones and the technology to manufacture them. It then claimed it was not a party to Russia’s war. President Zelensky rejects that fiction. By providing weapons used against Ukraine, the regime entered the conflict on Moscow’s side.
Russia has launched thousands of Shahed-type drones against Ukrainian homes, power stations, and other civilian infrastructure. Some were manufactured in Iran. Others are Russian-produced Gerans based on Iranian designs. They allow Moscow to sustain a relentless bombing campaign at relatively low cost.
Kyiv therefore has a clear interest in imposing costs on the military network supporting that campaign. Its target should be the regime’s military machinery and partnership with Russia – not the Iranian people, who have no say in either.
Ukraine Condemns Russian Move to Erase Borders With Occupied Areas
There is another reason Tehran is uneasy. Ukraine is much harder to intimidate than the governments the regime normally threatens.
The Arab states of the Persian Gulf have ports, refineries, financial centers, technology hubs, and carefully planned cities. A single missile or drone volley could inflict enormous economic damage. Even when these states possess the capacity to respond, they have powerful incentives to exercise restraint. Tehran cultivates and exploits that hesitation.
Ukraine does not fit this model. Its cities have already been battered. Its electrical grid has already been bombed. Its people are fighting for their national survival and independence. That is why President Zelensky worries Tehran. The regime’s most dangerous adversary is not necessarily the strongest. It is the one that cannot be intimidated into submission.
The Caspian Sea strike exposed a separate vulnerability.
As Iran’s southern waters face heavier American military pressure and naval restrictions, the Caspian basin has acquired greater strategic value. It provides Tehran with a northern corridor to Russia and Central Asia for commercial cargo, industrial supplies, military cooperation, and sanctions evasion.
Kyiv said the Iranian commercial ship was not deliberately targeted. But the strike demonstrated that Caspian traffic can no longer be treated as beyond Ukraine’s reach. If that corridor becomes contested, the cost of moving weapons, dual-use materials, and sanctioned cargo between the regime and Russia will rise. Tehran could face pressure on both its southern maritime routes and its northern military supply network.
President Zelensky should exploit this anxiety by accelerating and institutionalizing a strategy Ukraine has already begun.
Ukraine has spent years detecting and defeating Iranian-designed drones. It has also built a large domestic drone industry capable of producing effective systems at a fraction of the cost of traditional Western weapons. Ukrainian counter-drone experts have already assisted governments in the Middle East. Kyiv has also pursued longer-term defense cooperation with several Arab states of the Persian Gulf.
The next step is to bring Israel into this emerging framework and secure firm American backing.
Each partner offers a different comparative advantage. Ukraine brings battlefield experience and inexpensive interceptor drones. Israel brings advanced sensors, electronic warfare, intelligence, and air-defense technology. The Arab states of the Persian Gulf bring financing, industrial capacity, and a direct interest in protecting their infrastructure. The United States can provide coordination, advanced systems, production licenses, and political support.
President Zelensky should present this to President Donald Trump as an expansion of an existing strategy, not another request for open-ended assistance. Integrating Ukrainian production, Israeli technology, American power, and investment from the Persian Gulf states would reduce the cost of defending American forces and regional allies. In return, Kyiv should seek additional air-defense systems, joint-production agreements, financing, and stronger sanctions enforcement against the procurement networks serving Tehran and Moscow.
President Zelensky has already met twice with Prince Reza Pahlavi, who, in turn, gave a speech earlier this year in Ukraine. Both leaders have a vital interest in seeing political change in Iran.
Prince Reza Pahlavi represents an alternative strategic direction for the country. A free and democratic Iran would have no interest in arming Russia, threatening Ukraine’s partners, or spending Iranian wealth on foreign wars. It could instead become a natural partner of Ukraine, Israel, the United States, and the Arab states of the Persian Gulf.
Tehran calls President Zelensky a clown because acknowledging the real threat would be less comfortable. He leads a country that has learned to absorb punishment, innovate under pressure, and strike military networks once considered beyond its reach.
Ukraine, Israel, the United States, the Arab states of the Persian Gulf, and the Iranian people now have an opportunity to pull in the same direction. That is not a prospect Tehran finds amusing.

articles.title: Netanyahu hits London with ‘Islamic Britain’ jibe
articles.body:
Netanyahu hits London with ‘Islamic Britain’ jibe
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has described the UK as the “Islamic Republic of Britain,” as the country’s new Labour government weighs taking measures against Israel.
Speaking on an Israeli Army Radio podcast on Friday, Netanyahu criticized the British media’s coverage of Israel, while comparing it to reporting during the 1967 Six-Day War.
“Go find that in Britain today, which you could call the Islamic Republic of Britain,” he said, as cited by Israeli media.
Netanyahu then echoed a 2024 joke made by US Vice President J.D. Vance, saying Britain could become the first “Islamic republic with nuclear weapons.”
According to the latest census-based figures, Muslims account for around 6% of the UK’s population, while Pakistan, officially the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, has possessed nuclear weapons since the 1990s.
The British Foreign Office called the comments “completely unacceptable,” noting that the issue had been raised with the Israeli government.
Relations between London and Israel have deteriorated since the UK formally recognized the State of Palestine in September of 2025, a move rejected by Netanyahu’s government.
The exchange comes weeks after Andy Burnham became prime minister. Before taking office, Burnham said Labour “didn’t get it right” on Gaza, asserting that Britain needed to put greater pressure on the Israeli government, including through the use of sanctions and measures targeting trade with Israeli settlements.
Nonetheless, Britain has maintained military-export ties with Israel. While London did suspend some arms licenses in 2024 due to concerns that the equipment could be used to commit serious violations of international humanitarian law, it exempted components supplied through the multinational F-35 program.
Britain also provided military support during this year’s conflict with Iran. London deployed aircraft to intercept Iranian attacks and authorized US forces to use British bases for operations against Iranian missile launchers and related sites. British security cooperation with Israel has included surveillance flights over Gaza and intelligence sharing.
The remarks follow reports that there is growing frustration with Netanyahu in the US. Axios reported on Friday that President Donald Trump has declined to endorse Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s October election so far, despite being repeatedly asked about it. Earlier this month, the Israeli PM rejected a 15-point Gaza plan backed by Trump, while insisting that Israeli forces would not withdraw until Hamas was fully disarmed.

"Battlegroup Dnepr units inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade of the Ukrainian army, a National Guard brigade and a marine infantry brigade," the ministry said.
"Up to 220 Ukrainian military personnel, two armored combat vehicles, 107 motor vehicles, five field artillery guns and 12 electronic warfare stations were destroyed in that frontline area over the week," it said.
Russian air defenses intercept 7,078 Ukrainian UAVs, 64 smart bombs over week

"Air defense capabilities shot down 64 guided aerial bombs, 16 rockets of the US-made HIMARS and Czech-made Vampire multiple launch rocket systems, 8 Flamingo cruise missiles, 5 Neptune long-range missiles and 7,078 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.

Tally of Ukrainian army’s losses

articles.title: US Reaper losses mount as Iran war reshapes drone warfare
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US Reaper losses mount as Iran war reshapes drone warfare
The US military has lost around a quarter of its MQ-9 Reaper drone fleet during the war on Iran, a striking rate of attrition that comes as Washington increasingly turns towards cheaper, expendable drones designed to be deployed and lost at scale.
At least 45 Reapers have been lost since the conflict began, according to The Washington Post, out of a pre-war US fleet of around 185 aircraft.
But defence analyst Stacie Pettyjohn, director of the Defense Program at the Center for a New American Security, told The New Arab that the scale of the losses should not necessarily be seen as evidence that the Reapers had failed.
"It is a notable portion of the active MQ-9 fleet. But there was a decision that it was worth putting the Reapers at risk to assist with targeting of mobile Iranian drone and missile forces," she said.
"They can loiter overhead for more than 24 hours keeping watch over an area and if they are shot down, no one dies."
The MQ-9, which can conduct long-duration surveillance as well as strikes, costs tens of millions of dollars depending on its configuration. Its losses during the Iran war could therefore represent well over $1 billion worth of aircraft.
Pettyjohn said the US Air Force had already been seeking for years to reduce its reliance on the Reaper as it shifted away from counter-terrorism operations towards preparing for conflicts with major military powers.
"They still are expensive platforms, but given that they were able to help US forces execute important missions without the loss of life I would consider their losses, which were for a good reason, acceptable," she said.
Even if the losses were judged operationally acceptable, however, the destruction of around a quarter of the fleet in less than six months represents a major depletion of a costly US surveillance and strike capability, raising questions over how readily Washington could absorb or replace losses on that scale in a prolonged conflict.
The Reaper was developed and heavily used during US counter-terrorism campaigns in Afghanistan, Iraq and elsewhere, where Washington largely enjoyed air superiority and faced little threat to the aircraft themselves.
The war on Iran has instead pushed the platform into a far more contested environment, exposing vulnerabilities that have long been understood, which raises questions about the Trump administration's use of them.
Pettyjohn said the vulnerability of large unmanned aircraft such as the MQ-9 to modern air defences has long been recognised.
"I don't think anyone ever thought that the Reapers would be survivable against modern air defenses," she said, pointing to Ukraine's early success with Turkish-made Bayraktar TB2 drones before Russian air defences began operating more effectively.
"The US found a valuable role for MQ-9s against Iran but it entailed considerable risk. But in high-intensity modern wars there are going to be losses. Better they be uncrewed platforms."
The scale of those losses nevertheless underlines the cost of using high-end reusable drones in an environment where even unmanned aircraft can be destroyed in significant numbers.
The attrition comes as the US simultaneously expands its use of much cheaper unmanned weapons.
US Central Command announced this week the creation of Task Force Falcon Strike, its first multinational, multi-domain attack-drone force, which will operate one-way attack systems in the air, on the surface of the sea and underwater alongside regional partners.
The move builds on a broader Pentagon effort to field large numbers of inexpensive drones, reflecting lessons drawn from Ukraine, Russia and Iran.
Both Russia and Ukraine have deployed cheap first-person-view and one-way attack drones in significant numbers, while Iran has spent years developing relatively inexpensive systems such as the Shahed family that can be launched in massed attacks.
Those conflicts have demonstrated how lower-cost systems can impose significant military and financial pressure on forces relying on more expensive aircraft, missiles and air-defence interceptors, while also making battlefield losses routine rather than exceptional.
The experience has helped push militaries towards what is often described as "affordable mass": accepting that individual systems may be lost while possessing enough of them to sustain operations.
Pettyjohn said the Iran conflict had reinforced lessons already emerging from Ukraine "about affordable mass and the grim realities of modern warfare where there are many losses".
But she cautioned against treating cheap one-way attack drones as straightforward replacements for aircraft such as the Reaper.
"I think that they are complements. Cheap one-way attack drones are more like munitions. MQ-9s are intended to be used many times and fly many different munitions. That makes them in a different class of drone," she said.
Cheaper attack drones can also provide militaries with greater "magazine depth", allowing more weapons to be launched without rapidly exhausting stocks of expensive long-range missiles.
Yet their lower individual price does not always mean an attack will ultimately be cheaper.
"Cheap one-way attack drones provide additional magazine depth at much lower cost, but they do not offer the same capability as sophisticated missiles," Pettyjohn said.
"And you need many more of them to achieve the same effect, which means that their per salvo cost may be more expensive than high-end weapons."

articles.title: Zelensky Confirms Flamingo Missile Strikes Deep in Russian Territory
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on Saturday, Aug. 15, that Ukrainian forces executed long-range strikes targeting strategic facilities in Russia, including the use of “Flamingo“ missiles against an aerospace plant in the Samara region.
In a statement on Telegram, Zelensky detailed the outcomes of what he termed deep strikes into Russian territory.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He confirmed that the Progress Space Rocket Centre, a key enterprise within the Russian state corporation Roscosmos involved in electronics production, was struck in the Samara region.
Zelensky explicitly stated that “Flamingo” missiles were utilized for this attack, noting the facility is located approximately 900 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.
The president also reported that long-range weapons struck the Savasleyka airfield in the Nizhny Novgorod region. He specified that the base, situated roughly 700 kilometers from Ukraine, hosts aircraft used as carriers for Russian missiles targeting Ukrainian cities and villages.
Furthermore, Zelensky confirmed an attack on an oil facility in the port of Ust-Luga in the Leningrad region, located over 800 kilometers from the border, stating that the necessary damage to the target was recorded.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the “Progress” Rocket and Space Center in Samara. A direct hit on the target was confirmed, followed by a fire on the facility’s grounds.
Romania Reports Fourth Discovery of Drone Debris in 24 Hours
The “Progress” Rocket and Space Center is one of the key enterprises in the Russian Federation’s rocket and space industry, producing launch vehicles of the “Soyuz” family. These are used to launch Russian spacecraft for military, reconnaissance, and communications purposes into orbit.
In particular, the “Soyuz-2.1b” is used to deploy the Russian “Rassvet” satellite constellation – a broadband satellite communications system that Russia positions as an analogue to Starlink.
The Progress Rocket and Space Center also manufactures Earth observation satellites, which the enemy uses for reconnaissance purposes.
The extent of the damage is being assessed.
In addition, the Savasleika airfield in the Nizhny Novgorod region of the Russian Federation was struck. A direct hit on the target was recorded, followed by a fire on the airfield grounds.
“Savasleika” is used, in particular, to base and deploy MiG-31K interceptor fighters – carriers of the Kh-47M2 “Kinzhal” aeroballistic missiles.
Prior reports of Samara aerospace plant strikes
The presidential confirmation followed reports from earlier on Saturday regarding explosions at industrial aerospace enterprises in Samara.
Following the initial blasts, Denis Shtilerman, chief designer at the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, published footage depicting the launch of an FP-5 “Flamingo” missile.
Samara region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev reported a missile strike on an unnamed industrial facility, while Mayor Ivan Noskov stated that the city’s industrial infrastructure sustained localized damage.
Open-source intelligence analysts reviewing images of the site identified the location as the shared industrial zone of the Aviakor aviation plant and the Progress Space Rocket Centre. Progress manufactures Soyuz-2 carrier rockets and space satellites, while Aviakor produces and maintains aircraft.
Concurrent drone activity in Crimea
The strikes on Russian territory coincided with reports of drone activity in occupied Crimea on Saturday morning.
Local residents reported explosions in Sevastopol and the Bakhchysarai district. Following the blasts, local Telegram channels reported power outages in Sevastopol and a fire in the Balaklava area.
Russian occupation authorities did not issue an immediate statement regarding the incidents.

articles.title: US pulls last aircraft carrier in Asia as Trump focuses on Iran and the Western Hemisphere
articles.body:
US pulls last aircraft carrier in Asia as Trump focuses on Iran and the Western Hemisphere
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s war against Iran is stretching the limits of U.S. aircraft carriers and leaving the western Pacific without one of the key American warships as China shows more signs of aggression.
The USS George Washington is departing the Pacific and expected to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln in the Middle East amid growing concerns about mental health and supply issues aboard the long-deployed carrier. The Lincoln has had its time at sea extended from its original May return date to support operations against Iran.
The lack of a U.S. carrier in the Pacific may be short-lived if the Navy deploys another in the next couple of months. But it shows how the open-ended operations with Iran are running some American sailors ragged, analysts say, while the Trump administration further retreats from the Asia-Pacific region and focuses on the Western Hemisphere.
“The administration says that the Pacific is supposed to be the most important behind the Western Hemisphere,” said Greg Poling, director of the Southeast Asia Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Instead, the U.S. is “doing the exact opposite” of its previously expressed goal of pulling out of the Middle East.
American allies in the Pacific are unsettled over the unpredictability of the Republican administration, Poling said, while Beijing “is quite happy with U.S. distraction, with the frustration of U.S. allies and partners.”
China may take advantage of US carrier’s absence
Beijing sees the U.S. military presence in the region as a threat to China’s rise and an obstacle to its ambition to seize Taiwan, the self-governing island it claims as its own. But the United States has argued that the Pacific region is too important economically to lose.
No one expects China to invade Taiwan because an American aircraft carrier has left the region. But the carrier’s absence gives the Chinese another opportunity to show its strength, said Bryan Clark, a former Navy submariner who is a defense analyst at the Hudson Institute.
“They’re using this as part of the narrative to demonstrate to the Philippines, to Japan, to Indonesia and others that the U.S. is not the big dog in the western Pacific anymore,” Clark said. “They would just prefer that countries in the region decide that China is the bigger power and the U.S. is not able to guarantee their security anymore.”
China conducted naval exercises this week with Indonesia and recently has shown signs of aggression toward Japan and the Philippines, two key U.S. allies that also have territorial disputes with Beijing.
China carried out military drills this month near the Scarborough Shoal in the South China Sea. Both China and the Philippines have claims over the shoal. Last month, a Chinese guided-missile destroyer conducted a live-fire exercise off Japan’s southernmost island of Okinotori.
Adm. Frank Bradley, head of the U.S. Special Operations Command, has been trying to reassure regional allies of Washington’s commitment. He was in Manila on Thursday, telling his Filipino counterparts that U.S. special operations forces are ready to step up joint exercises to strengthen the countries’ alliance. He also is expected to travel to Japan.
Evan Sankey, a policy analyst at the Cato Institute who focuses on U.S. policy toward China, said aircraft carriers provide psychological assurance to U.S. allies. The absence of carriers in the region, he said, “adds to the general sense that the U.S. is distracted by events in the Middle East.”
Trump has relied on aircraft carriers for military actions
Trump has relied heavily on aircraft carriers to support military operations during his second term. For example, the USS Gerald R. Ford returned home in mid-May after an 11-month deployment, the longest since the Vietnam War, during which it supported the U.S. fight against Iran and the capture of Venezuela’s then-leader, Nicolás Maduro.
The Ford had experienced a fire in a laundry space that forced the carrier to turn around and return to the Mediterranean Sea for repairs and left hundreds of sailors without places to sleep. Meanwhile, the Lincoln has spent a record uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days. Democratic lawmakers have been calling for investigations and greater visibility into conditions aboard the ship.
Warships and their crews can only handle so much, said Robert Farley, who teaches national security and diplomacy at the University of Kentucky and often writes about aircraft carriers.
“People don’t get enough rest. It’s psychologically exhausting. And R&R is part of keeping the crew healthy,” Farley said. “Sometimes it’s framed as, ‘These people haven’t had a vacation.’ But we are dealing with well-known limits on the capacity of a crew to operate at top efficiency over time. And that just declines.”
Clark, of the Hudson Institute, said the squeeze on the nation’s aircraft carriers stems from the lack of preparation and planning for the Iran war.
“If we were going to mobilize to do this kind of conflict, and we anticipated it might go this long, we might have done some changes to the carrier schedule to make sure more would be available,” Clark said.
Clark said the Navy has 11 aircraft carriers and typically deploys two or three at a time. But it could soon deploy four if the USS Theodore Roosevelt leaves San Diego for the Middle East, allowing the Washington to return to Pacific.
But the massive warships will need maintenance, likely causing a bottleneck at the nation’s only two carrier shipyards.
“We’ll end up with a maintenance debt that needs to be paid for the next few years,” Clark said. “We’ll probably have less carrier presence than we’ve had in the previous years because carriers will be lined up to get into the shipyard.”
There are questions about the use of aircraft carriers in modern warfare
Michael Swaine, a senior research fellow in the Quincy Institute’s East Asia Program, questions the future need for aircraft carriers as warfare rapidly changes.
Carriers can be more easily targeted with drones and missiles, particularly by an adversary such as China, Swaine said, while smaller ships and submarines can be as effective in striking targets as the fighter jets that launch off a carrier.
Top Navy officials have indicated a desire to move away from a heavy reliance on carriers. Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, told The Associated Press in February that he wants to convince commanders to use smaller, newer ships and other assets instead of consistently turning to huge aircraft carriers.

articles.title: Poland Holds Largest Military Parade Amid Major Defense Buildup
articles.body:
Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that “only those who are strong” will avoid war as Poland hosted its largest ever military parade amid a military buildup by Warsaw designed to strengthen NATO’s eastern flank against the threat from Russia.
Saturday’s display of the country’s military potential on land, sea and in the air comes on Poland’s Armed Forces Day, which marks the anniversary of a key Polish victory over the Soviet Union in the 1920 Battle of Warsaw.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The parade in Warsaw kicked off at noon, with more than 60 military aircraft flying over the Polish capital, followed by a ceremony which saw President Karol Nawrocki confer promotions on 21 Polish military officers.
The main portion of the parade started shortly afterwards – following speeches by Nawrocki and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz – with close to 2,000 Polish troops beginning their march along Warsaw’s Vistula River alongside more than 300 military vehicles.
With Russia’s war against Ukraine ongoing, effective deterrence is the key message behind this year’s parade as Poland accelerates its modernization program. The country, the biggest defense spender in NATO last year in relation to its GDP, has poured billions into new hardware including aircraft, ships and helicopters.
A naval parade involving more than 20 vessels, including ships from allied countries, is also being held near the cities of Gdynia and Gdańsk on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast, with Prime Minister Tusk in attendance.
How Europe’s Political Center Lost Its Voters - Why Meloni, Le Pen, and the AfD Are No Longer on the Margins
Call for strength
Speaking at the event, Tusk said that Poland wants to “avoid war”, and that “only those who are strong, well-prepared, truly independent and sovereign will avoid war.”
Other ceremonies were also held on Saturday as part of Armed Forces Day, including a ceremonial changing of the guard at Warsaw’s Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, attended by top officials.
President Nawrocki said that Poland, often attacked by its neighbors in its history, “knows perfectly well the price paid for independence and freedom.”

Spending spree

Poland spent around 4.7% of GDP on defense in 2025, the highest relative figure among NATO members, and aims to raise spending to 5% in 2026.
Poland’s armed forces now have more than 220,000 active duty personnel, making it the third largest military in NATO, behind only the US and Turkey. Warsaw is targeting 500,000 service members, including 200,000 reservists, by 2039.

Russia's defense ministry threatens to "freeze" Ukraine this winter. Moscow posted photos of attack drones captioned "like snow on your head," tying the taunt to its strikes on Ukraine's ports.
Poland was ready to scrap these MiG-29s. Bulgaria's interest just revived the Ukraine deal.. Warsaw was ready to let the jets go to the scrapyard, until a rival buyer showed up.
745 km² recaptured in Ukraine's eight-month Oleksandrivka counteroffensive, Kyiv says. The eight-month operation retook 26 villages across three oblasts, halting Russia's push toward Dnipropetrovsk and turning it back on Ukrainian soil, per the report.
Ukrainian drones hit Wildberries warehouse in Tver for the third time in two weeks. Wall damaged again, no injuries reported, marketplace says goods intact.
Ukrainian drones hit Russia's Ust-Luga oil port for the 6th time this year. Fire breaks out at Baltic terminal handling nearly half of Russia's regional exports.
Intelligence and technology
Captured Akhmat fighter says he chose Ukraine and a drone guided him away from Russia's ranks. Magomed said earlier Chechen defections prompted Russian commanders to check fighters' phones and tighten surveillance.
Armor can barely reach Ukraine's front now—so robots drive and soldiers walk. Ukraine's frontline logistics are under strain from drone pressure, forcing soldiers to walk while ground robots take over the most dangerous runs.
They find a sword, we find a shield: Ukrainian soldier on why drones will never replace infantry. He went from mortarman to drone operator, and says neither role can absorb the other.

articles.title: Days until MoU deadline as US and Iran claim Hormuz control
articles.body:
The live blog is now over and will be back tomorrow at 9am BST. You can read more of The New Arab's coverage of the region here.
Breadcrumb
The live page is now closed.
Here were the key updates of the day:
And so we continue our live coverage of the day...
Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said early Saturday that Tehran would not be intimidated by threats or a show of force by Washington after US President Donald Trump said he would declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory.
Commenting on Trump's statements, Gharibabadi said in a post on X that the strategic waterway would only be opened or closed under Iran's authority.
UAE's Abu Dhabi National Oil Company said on Saturday that one of its vessels came under attack while transiting the Strait of Hormuz a day earlier.
The state oil company said no injuries were reported, with the situation now under control.
Britain on Friday hit back at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu derisively calling the country an "Islamic republic" in an interview, branding the remarks "completely unacceptable".
The diplomatic tit-for-tat came after the right-wing prime minister made the reference in an army radio podcast interview the previous day, in which he criticised the UK's stance on Israel.
It echoed the language of far-right politicians and commentators in the Western world who have made baseless claims that parts of Britain have come under Islamic law due to immigration, drawing accusations of Islamophobia.
"These comments are completely unacceptable and we have raised them with the Israeli Government," a UK government spokesman said Friday.
President Donald Trump on Friday said he would "soon" declare the Strait of Hormuz waterway part of US territory after defeating Iran.
"After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated -- pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," he said with a chuckle during a political rally at a police academy in New York state.
"It's true," he added.
Trump, together with Israel, launched a war against Iran on 28 February but remains locked in a stalemate with Iran over the strait, with Iran denying access to much of the civilian shipping and the US Navy mounting a blockade of Iranian ports in an attempt to cripple its economy.
"We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to," Trump the cheering crowd of supporters and police.
US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Friday that the United States will hit Iran hard economically as Washington and Tehran struggle to reach a deal to end a nearly six-month conflict.
His comments came a day after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US was going to apply measures that have "never been seen" on Tehran as soon as next week.
A military official from Yemen's internationally recognised government said a Houthi attack on Friday on the port city of Mokha killed six people, two of them security personnel.
The Iran-backed rebels "fired five missiles at commercial ships unloading at the port, and two ships are on fire", the official said.
Israeli settlers shot two Palestinians in the occupied West Bank town of Bani Na'im, east of Hebron, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa, citing the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.
Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem on Friday accused Lebanese authorities of subjecting the country's armed forces to undue pressure by implementing a framework deal agreed with Israel to end hostilities.
The June trilateral framework, to which the United States is also a party, involves the disarmament of the Lebanese militant group and a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon's south, where it has occupied several areas.
It also includes the deployment of the Lebanese army to areas where Israel's military has pulled out, starting in test areas known as "pilot zones".
"How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?" Qassem said in a speech.
In talks between Lebanon and Israel in Rome last week, both sides discussed which countries might participate in a committee tasked with verifying the Lebanese army's deployment in the pilot zones and clearance of Hezbollah weapons and infrastructure, a Lebanese presidency source told AFP.
"Israel is attempting to bind Lebanon to an inquiry committee that oversees the army's deployment, operations, and internal details. Where is the patriotism? Where is the dignity of the army that ought to be preserved?" said Qassem.
Yemen's Houthis said they targeted an Aramco facility in the Saudi city of Najran with a drone, the group-run SABA news agency reported on Friday, citing a military source.
The source said the attack was in response to what it described as Saudi military aircraft violating Yemen's sovereignty by entering airspace over the northeastern part of Saada governorate.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities or Aramco. It was not immediately clear from the report whether the facility was hit.
US President Donald Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner will visit Israel next week in hopes of bridging gaps on a Gaza plan rejected by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, officials said Friday.
Kushner and Nickolay Mladenov, the high representative for Gaza of Trump's so-called Board of Peace implementing the deal, will visit both Israel and key mediator Egypt.
The trip comes after Netanyahu publicly rejected a 15-point plan announced by Mladenov in which Hamas agreed to hand over its weapons to a new Palestinian governing committee in Gaza.
A Board of Peace official said Kushner and Mladenov hoped for "constructive conversations" on advancing Trump's overall peace plan that began with the October 2025 declaration of a ceasefire, which has reduced but not ended Israeli strikes in Gaza.
"The United States and Israel agree on the end state, which is a demilitarised Hamas," the official said on condition of anonymity.
"We will hear the concerns that have been raised and talk about next steps. What is critical is that we both agree on the desired outcome and are finding ways to accelerate progress."
The French embassy in Israel has called on the Israeli government to arrest and charge violent settlers in the occupied West Bank, saying in a post on X that the government must "take all necessary measures to protect the Palestinian civilian population, as required of them under international law," according to Haaretz.
The embassy added that it "call[s] on the Israeli authorities to arrest the perpetrators of these acts and bring them to justice."
Israeli forces and settlers continued their assault against Palestinian communities across the occupied West Bank on Friday despite mounting international condemnation over the siege of homes in Qusra and escalating attacks elsewhere.
In Qusra, south of Nablus, settlers remained near Palestinian homes for a sixth consecutive day, while Israeli forces prevented foreign and Israeli solidarity activists from reaching besieged families with water and other basic supplies.
The siege has drawn unusually sharp criticism from Washington, with White House officials pressing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly condemn the settlers after learning that one of the affected homes belongs to a Palestinian American.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee - a supporter of the settler movement - described those responsible as "Israeli terrorists" and their actions as "criminal", while France condemned what it called the "occupation" of Palestinian homes and called on Israeli authorities to arrest and prosecute those responsible.
Amid the criticism, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz ordered the military to prepare a plan to transfer civilian law enforcement in the occupied West Bank to the police.
Egypt is seriously considering joining the new joint defence agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said on Thursday.
Abdelatty made the remarks after talks with his Turkish counterpart, Hakan Fidan, in the northern coastal city of El Alamein.
Asked at a joint press conference whether Cairo would enter the agreement, Abdelatty said the pact was being examined by the relevant Egyptian authorities in accordance with the constitution and any legal obligations that membership could entail.
The agreement, known as the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, was signed last Friday by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
It includes a collective defence provision modelled on NATO’s Article 5, under which an attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all three.
Iraq's average daily oil exports since the beginning of August are the highest since the outbreak of the Middle East war between Iran and the United States choked off the Strait of Hormuz, the oil ministry said Friday.
Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair told a press conference that "exports since the beginning of the month have reached a rate of two million barrels" per day, for a total of around 26 million barrels.
He said the daily rate had been achieved "for the first time since the crisis began" on February 28 after US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which retaliated by blocking the waterway crucial for global oil and gas trade.
Before the war, Iraq produced around four million barrels per day, and exported an average of 105 million barrels per month, mostly from its Basra oil terminal via Hormuz.
Ali Nizar, the head of Iraq's State Organisation for Marketing of Oil (SOMO), said in a TV interview last week that Iraq exported in July "35.5 to 37 million barrels" via Hormuz.
Israel's defence minister called Friday for the police to take over law enforcement in the occupied West Bank from the military, which has come under fire from the right-wing for trying to remove settlers harassing Palestinians.
The measure, if implemented, would be a step towards Israeli annexation of the occupied Palestinian territory - something several ministers in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government openly call for.
Defence Minister Israel Katz's office announced he had "instructed the IDF to prepare a plan to transfer all enforcement powers regarding civil matters among Israeli communities and population in Judea and Samaria to the Israel Police," using the Biblical term for the illegally occupied West Bank.
The military would continue to exercise power over Palestinian residents of the West Bank.
"The IDF's role is to fight Palestinian terrorism, focus on defending borders and communities against threats... and not chase boys on the hilltops," Katz said, referring to the Hilltop Youth - a settler group regularly accused of violence towards Palestinians.
