articles.title: Raid Hunter: Northrop’s new gun-based air defense system
articles.body:
- Northrop Grumman unveiled Raid Hunter, a 50mm gun-based air defense system, on Aug. 11 to counter cruise missiles and drone swarms.
- The system uses a guided 50mm round derived from a Navy-funded 57mm program and can be transported by C-130 aircraft.
U.S. defense giant Northrop Grumman unveiled Raid Hunter on Aug. 11, a 50mm gun-based air defense system built to counter cruise missiles and drone swarms at short range around military bases and other critical sites.
The system pairs the company’s XM913 Bushmaster III chain gun with newly developed precision-guided 50mm ammunition and a networked system controller for battle management, Northrop Grumman said. It is designed to defeat “high-volume, mixed-threat aerial raids,” engaging multiple targets in rapid succession rather than the single-target engagements typical of most short-range air defense systems.
“Raid Hunter addresses a critical short-range defense gap by delivering rapid, high-capacity protection against complex, mass aerial threats like cruise missiles and drone swarms,” said Kenn Todorov, vice president and general manager for command and control and weapons integration at Northrop Grumman. “It provides warfighters with a cost-effective, flexible tool to decisively defeat evolving threats now and in the future, strengthening the security of vital bases and infrastructure.”
The current version is palletized for transport aboard C-130 aircraft, with vehicle-mounted and container-based configurations planned for the future. Northrop Grumman said the system is already undergoing testing, with additional trials planned through the rest of the year to validate performance and support faster fielding. The company positions Raid Hunter within its broader Raid Defense Solutions portfolio, intended to work alongside its other air defense systems in a layered architecture.
Northrop Grumman says the 50mm caliber provides “lethal, cost-considerate engagement with deep magazines and fast reloads,” aiming to address the cost mismatch between expensive interceptors and cheap drone threats. Company officials told Warsight that guided ammunition also extends the system’s effective range and reduces dispersion at longer distances compared with unguided rounds, since the round corrects its own course rather than relying purely on the accuracy of the initial shot.
Northrop Grumman’s initial announcement included little imagery of the system, an absence noted by Sam Cranny-Evans, editor of Calibre Defence, on social media. Earlier photos of a scale model exist from Eurosatory 2026 in June, where Northrop Grumman first showed the then-unnamed concept and where Warsight editor Mark Cazalet interviewed company officials about the design.
At Eurosatory, Northrop Grumman displayed the system as a palletized turret fitted with a radar for target acquisition and an optoelectronic sight for fire control, armed with the XM913 cannon chambered in 50x228mm ammunition, dubbed “Supershot,” with 400 ready rounds, according to Warsight‘s reporting. Company officials told Warsight the guided 50mm round builds on a separate, Navy-funded program to develop a guided 57mm round for the Mk 110 remote weapon station used on littoral combat ships. Northrop Grumman has not disclosed the guided round’s seeker type, saying only that testing results have been positive.
Company representatives told Warsight that two of the palletized units fit on a single C-130 and can also be moved by CH-47 Chinook helicopter, and that four to six units could provide 360-degree coverage at a large airfield. The system is designed to integrate with the Integrated Battle Command System, allowing it to work alongside longer-range interceptors such as Patriot, IRIS-T and NASAMS, engaging threats those systems let through.
Beyond the Navy-funded 57mm work, Northrop Grumman said it is in discussions with the Army and other potential customers about the 50mm system, though the company has not disclosed any procurement contracts or timelines for Raid Hunter beyond the ongoing test schedule.

articles.title: Royal Navy drone warship fleet could triple missile capacity
articles.body:
War games examining the Royal Navy’s planned shift towards crewed and uncrewed systems are claimed to have produced roughly three times the missile capacity for a North Atlantic conflict, according to a former senior Royal Navy officer.
War games examining the Royal Navy’s planned Hybrid Navy concept are claimed to have produced a substantial increase in combat mass and roughly three times the missile capacity available for a North Atlantic conflict, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The assessment comes from Rear Admiral (retired) James Parkin CB CBE, a former Royal Navy Director Develop, writing for the Council on Geostrategy’s Britain’s World magazine. Parkin argues that the combination of high-end crewed warships with larger numbers of autonomous and remotely operated systems offers one of the few realistic routes to increasing naval mass without a corresponding rise in personnel or the cost associated with building additional major warships.
He writes that testing of the concept through hybrid war games has produced what he describes as a substantial increase in combat mass and “roughly threefold missile capacity for a North Atlantic contest”. The figure is presented as a claimed result of war gaming rather than an operationally demonstrated capability, but it provides an indication of the scale of effect being sought through the Royal Navy’s future force structure.
The Hybrid Navy concept was formalised in the 2025 Strategic Defence Review, which envisaged highly capable crewed submarines, warships and aircraft operating alongside much larger numbers of uncrewed systems. The 2026 Defence Investment Plan subsequently described a network of crewed ships and uncrewed surface and underwater vessels connected through a Maritime Fighting Web, alongside plans for at least six Common Combat Vessels and autonomous collaborative aircraft under Projects VANQUISH and PANTHEON.
Parkin argues that the concept should not be interpreted as a replacement for conventional warships. He warns against drawing direct conclusions from Ukraine’s use of uncrewed vessels in the Black Sea, distinguishing between sea denial in a relatively enclosed maritime environment and the sea control required by Britain and NATO across the North Atlantic.
He writes: “Cheap, massed, and precise systems matter, but Britain must protect oceanic trade routes, nuclear-power ballistic missile submarine (SSBN) bastions, and NATO strike groups operating far from friendly ports.” Parkin argues that the Hybrid Navy must therefore remain centred on high-end crewed platforms, with uncrewed systems providing additional sensing, weapons capacity and persistent presence.
The memorandum also identifies regulatory constraints as a potentially significant obstacle. According to Parkin, the permissions required to operate uncrewed surface vessels larger than 24 metres routinely in British waters have yet to be established. He states that no uncrewed vessel above that size has so far received either Maritime and Coastguard Agency or Defence Maritime Regulator operating clearance, while neither civilian classification societies nor the Naval Authority and Technical Group have approved such a design.
Parkin argues that addressing this will require more than changes to individual regulations, calling instead for Defence to make greater use of the freedoms already available to it to conduct experimentation. He advocates giving operators greater scope to “learn by doing” and to fail safely during development rather than allowing lengthy approval processes to slow experimentation with new systems.
A second issue identified is the speed at which lessons from trials and operations are fed back into equipment development. Parkin contrasts traditional British defence acquisition cycles, which he says can take months or years to incorporate changes, with the much faster development cycle seen in Ukraine. He cites the so-called “rule of six”: six hours for operator feedback to reach a manufacturer, six days for software updates, six weeks for hardware modifications and six months to replace a system entirely where necessary.
The memorandum argues that a similar continuous feedback model will be required if the Hybrid Navy is to deliver the intended increase in mass and weapons capacity. Parkin also warns that the programme will require specialist maritime knowledge throughout acquisition and development, rather than treating the transition primarily as a conventional programme-management exercise.
The Royal Navy’s underlying challenge is one of numbers and cost as Parkin notes that large complex European warships can now cost around £2 billion to £2.5 billion per hull, while specialised naval aircraft can approach £100 million each. Against that background, the Hybrid Navy is intended to distribute functions traditionally concentrated aboard individual ships across a much larger network of crewed and uncrewed platforms.
Parkin served in the Royal Navy for 28 years and was Director Develop in Navy Command Headquarters between 2021 and 2025. His assessment is presented as analysis rather than an official Ministry of Defence statement, but it sets out both the potential operational gains and the regulatory, cultural and acquisition challenges involved in turning the Hybrid Navy concept into a deployable force.

articles.title: “Responsibility is inevitable”: Zelenskyy warns Russian collaborators in occupied territories after explosion kills defector
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian special services are conducting targeted operations against collaborators in Russian-occupied territories who assist Russia’s attacks against Ukraine and Ukrainians.
Speaking after a meeting of Ukraine’s top military leadership on 14 August, Zelenskyy said he received a separate briefing from Ukraine’s special services on the progress of these operations.
He specifically mentioned occupied Sevastopol, where Ukrainian officials have previously accused local collaborators of supporting Russia’s military operations.
“Responsibility for collaborators is inevitable,” Zelenskyy said.
Operations target those helping Russia
Zelenskyy did not identify the individuals targeted or provide operational details, saying only that the special services had reported on the implementation of “targeted operations” against collaborators in occupied territories.
He said the targets include people who participate in Russian attacks against Ukraine and Ukrainians.
The comments signal that Ukraine is continuing to pursue individuals in occupied territory who assist Russian forces, including through intelligence, military support, or other forms of cooperation.
Sevastopol explosion on 13 August
The statement comes shortly after an explosion in occupied Sevastopol on 13 August killed a Russian military officer.
Russian and Ukrainian sources have circulated claims that the victim was Robert Shageyev, reportedly a former Ukrainian Navy officer who joined Russia after the occupation of Crimea and later served in Russia’s Black Sea Fleet.
His identity and the circumstances of the explosion have not been officially confirmed by Ukrainian authorities.
Russian sources had suggested Ukrainian involvement in the incident, but Ukraine has not publicly claimed responsibility.
Ukraine prepares for Russia’s next moves
The discussion of operations against collaborators was part of a broader meeting focused on Ukraine’s military preparations for the coming months.
Zelenskyy said the main issue was securing funding for Ukraine’s defense and security forces through the fall and winter. Officials identified funding gaps and additional requirements for expanding production of advanced weapons.
Among the priorities are faster production of Ukrainian strike weapons and new defensive systems, including jet-powered interceptor drones designed to counter Russian aerial threats.
Ukrainian intelligence also provided updated information about Russia’s plans, according to Zelenskyy. He said Ukraine is preparing countermeasures, including asymmetric responses.
The meeting also covered the effectiveness of Ukraine’s long-range and medium-range sanctions against Russia. Zelenskyy said the existing sanctions plan is being implemented and that priorities are being adjusted to ensure Ukraine has the capabilities needed to achieve its objectives.

articles.body:
President announces new sanctions targeting Russia's defense industry and financial networks
President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in his nightly video address, according to Ukrinform.
"Our sanctions against Russian oil refineries and other facilities in Russia's oil sector, our mid-range strikes against Russian military logistics, and our operation in the waters of the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov – all of this is working to limit Russia's war potential. It is important to continue this with more active political and legal measures as well," he said.
He recalled that Ukraine had imposed a sanctions package today targeting companies and vessels involved in exporting grain and other goods stolen in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
"We are preparing new sanctions packages against Russia's war industry, financial chains, and intermediaries. Unfortunately, a significant number of Russian enterprises working for the war are still not under international sanctions, and this must be corrected during August and September. We will raise this with leaders at all working levels," Zelensky said.
He also emphasized a direct task for Ukrainian diplomats: "In major jurisdictions around the world, sanctions are imposed on those Russian companies and individuals, as well as those who help Russia, whose influence truly matters in terms of prolonging this war and producing Russian missiles and drones."

articles.title: Military analyst: USA has cleaned out Patriot missile stockpiles of its European allies
articles.body:
News of the story 
        
                "On Point"
        
    
                                                                          
            
                                                                              
            
                        MINSK, 14 August (BelTA) – The United States of America has stripped European arsenals of Patriot missiles to replenish its own stock. Aleksandr Alesin, an independent military analyst, made the statement in a recent episode of BelTA’s project On Point.
 
The military analyst noted that according to some sources, the United States has about 800 missiles for Patriot air defense systems. The stock of these munitions has been depleted due to the war in the Middle East where these systems are used to intercept Iranian strikes. Aleksandr Alesin pointed out that because of that the USA has to remove Patriot missiles from the arsenals of its European allies.
 
“The USA has stripped the arsenals of Patriot missiles from its European allies. It left missiles with questionable shelf life and expired service life. Nobody can guarantee that they will even be able to take off and intercept anything,” he stated. “Apart from that, their total number makes up several dozens.”
 
The military analyst believes that the circumstances make Kiev’s chances of receiving missiles for Patriot air defense systems virtually zero, especially when it comes to the most advanced PAC-3 munitions. “Kiev can receive missiles of another class that can hit aeroballistic targets. Such missiles are produced in France, the UK, and Germany. But they can handle only ordinary ballistics. Even then about three missiles per warhead are required in such cases,” Aleksandr Alesin concluded.

articles.title: Russia Delays New Mobilization Wave Despite Rising Troop Losses
articles.body:
The Kremlin currently has no plans to initiate a new mobilization wave despite growing frontline losses and troop shortages, The Guardian reported, citing sources familiar with internal Russian discussions.
There are no indications that Russian President Vladimir Putin has authorized a new large-scale draft. An unnamed Western official confirmed the absence of preparations for a mobilization.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Kremlin is reportedly relying on volunteer recruitment through Ministry of Defense contracts to avoid the political risks associated with forced conscription.
However, human rights advocate Alexei Tabalov stated that finding individuals willing to fight is becoming increasingly difficult, despite significant financial incentives.
An employee of a Russian recruiting agency confirmed this trend, stating that the organization is required to recruit 20 to 30 men per month to avoid financial penalties. The recruiter, speaking anonymously, noted that meeting these quotas has become harder compared to the previous year.
While internal discussions about a potential mobilization occur, the recruiter said there are no official orders or signs of an imminent draft.
Risks of a second mobilization
International analysts suggest that a large-scale mobilization carries significant risks for the Russian government.
Commentary published by the German business daily Handelsblatt indicated that a new draft could negatively impact the Russian economy by removing more workers from the labor force and could lead to public dissatisfaction, similar to the reaction following the initial mobilization in September 2022.
Russia Admits New Petrol Shortages as Ukrainian Strikes Hit Refineries
Reports suggest Moscow is seeking alternative methods to bolster its forces without resorting to a domestic draft.
According to the Polish daily Rzeczpospolita, North Korea has deployed between 30,000 and 50,000 troops to Russia.
Analysts indicate this deployment is intended to provide the Kremlin with additional personnel and delay the necessity of a second mobilization wave.

articles.title: Putin Orders Military Leadership to Destroy NATO and the EU from Within — NYT
articles.body:
In late 2025, Russian dictator Vladimir Putin convened a briefing with military leaders and set a goal for 2026: “to dismantle NATO and the EU from within.”
This was reported by The New York Times, citing officials from both countries familiar with the details of the meeting.
According to the newspaper’s sources, Moldova plays a key role in these plans. According to representatives of Western intelligence agencies, subjugating Ukraine ranks first on Russia’s list of priorities, while establishing control over Moldova ranks second.
According to the newspaper’s sources, Moldova could serve as an ideal springboard for Russia to launch further aggression against both Ukraine and the West. They added that Putin still intends to seize territories in southern Ukraine to create a land corridor connecting Russia with Moldova.
To achieve these goals, Russia, in particular, attempted to interfere in the parliamentary elections held in Moldova on September 28, 2025—through cyberattacks, disinformation, as well as vote-buying and campaigning.
Moldovan priests were also recruited for the Kremlin’s campaign; in exchange for a thousand dollars, they were tasked with persuading parishioners to reject the referendum on Moldova’s accession to the European Union and to oppose pro-Western policies.
In addition, in the summer of 2025, the Russians organized a “training camp” in Serbia, where participants—mostly Moldovan citizens—were taught how to handle rifles, break through police cordons, and set buildings on fire.
Participants were paid $400 each to take part in the three- to four-day course. The camp’s instructors were personnel linked to Russian military intelligence (GRU). The goal of the camp was to train a group of fighters capable of interfering in elections, according to representatives of Western intelligence services.
Similar camps were organized in Bosnia and near Moscow. More than 100 young Moldovan citizens went through these camps. During their training, they were taught to manufacture and use incendiary devices and homemade explosive devices, as well as to operate drones “equipped with special devices for explosives or arson.”
After completing their training, some of the recruits were sent to the city of Banja Luka in Bosnia to carry out practical tasks—specifically, mapping the locations of administrative and government buildings and scouting potential sites for launching drones.
However, a few weeks before the vote, Moldovan police raided hundreds of homes and detained those who had undergone training at the camps, while Moldovan cybersecurity experts, with the support of Western allies, repelled the cyberattacks.
According to the investigation, the Moldovan prosecutor’s office is investigating the activities of more than 80 individuals suspected of inciting mass unrest. Twelve of them have already been formally charged. According to court records, participants were told that if she won, “war would break out in the country, just like in Ukraine.”
At least two individuals linked to these training camps are also suspected of involvement in other destabilization operations in France and Germany.

articles.title: Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon kill 11 in worst toll since June truce
articles.body:
Eleven people have been killed, including three children, and 19 injured in two Israeli airstrikes on southern Lebanon, the worst toll since deals in June brought a lull in hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah.
Israeli warplanes bombed a home on the outskirts of the village of Ansar, killing seven people and flattening the building early on Saturday morning. Rescue services were working at the site to try to find survivors and locate bodies.
Another airstrike hours later on a home in the town of Deir al-Zahrani killed two, wounded nine and covered the streets in rubble and smoke. An Israeli drone also targeted a motorcycle in the nearby city of Nabatieh, but it was unclear if the driver was killed.
The escalation came despite a June ceasefire in which most fighting between Israel and Hezbollah ended.
Residents of southern Lebanon wondered if the attacks signalled further escalation to come or if it was safe to stay in their homes. Neither village was in Israel’s self-declared “security zone” – a 231-square-mile area occupied by its forces.
The roads out of Nabatieh and the surrounding villages were choked with traffic after the strikes as people fled north in search of safety.
The Israeli military spokesperson, Ella Waweya, said Israel had attacked “Hezbollah infrastructure” in the Ansar and Nabatieh area in response to the group’s fighters attacking soldiers in the Ali Taher area.
Ali Taher is a hill where the Israeli military says large underground Hezbollah command and control centres are located, and it has been shelling the area for months.
The Lebanese prime minister, Nawaf Salam, condemned the Israeli attacks, calling them “extremely dangerous” and said they undermined efforts to establish stability in the south.
He called on Israel to stop the escalation. “The seven martyrs of the Israeli strike on the town of Ansar were not ‘military infrastructure’ and the children and women killed were not military targets,” he said.
Hezbollah condemned the attacks in a statement and said they would be met with a response. The group also accused the Lebanese government of serving Israel’s interests by negotiating with it.
“The Israeli enemy must clearly understand that its attacks, violations and attempts to impose a fait accompli cannot continue, and will be met with an appropriate response in defence of Lebanon,” Hezbollah’s media relations department said.
The latest round of fighting in Lebanon started after Hezbollah struck Israel with rockets on 2 March in retaliation for the killing of Iran’s supreme leader. Israel responded with an aerial campaign and invasion that killed more than 4,300 people and occupied about 6% of the country’s territory.
Violence has significantly decreased since the signing of a US-Iran memorandum of understanding in June on the broader Middle East war, and a US-sponsored framework deal between Lebanon and Israel agreed later that month.
But Lebanon still reports intermittent Israeli strikes occasionally causing casualties, and the broad demolitions of civilian buildings in southern villages and towns.
The news agency NNA said “the valley between Ansar and Zarariyeh was also subjected to a strike, the first at this geographical depth since the ceasefire two months ago”.
It also said “Israeli warplanes carried out a series of airstrikes targeting the Ali al-Taher ridge”. The news agency said Israeli forces detonated homes in the town of Bint Jbeil near the border.
The Israel-Lebanon framework deal includes the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from south Lebanon, and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in “pilot zones”.
On Friday, Hezbollah’s chief, Naim Qassem, accused Lebanese authorities of subjecting the country’s armed forces to undue pressure by implementing the deal. “How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?” he said.
This week, Human Rights Watch urged the UN to keep an international force in Lebanon after its peacekeepers’ mandate ends this year, saying “peacekeepers are a crucial deterrent against attacks on civilians and human rights abuses”.

articles.title: The first proxy war against Russia? Britain in the Caucasus
articles.body:
Britain’s forgotten proxy war against Russia
What is there in common between Ukrainians and the highlanders of the Caucasus, and what parallels can be drawn between Russia and Great Britain in the 19th century, and these same countries in the 21st century? In the 19th century, the British Empire fought against the Russian Empire using the highlanders in the Caucasus in a way that’s very similar to how Britain is now using Ukrainians.
In the 19th century, the Russian and British empires clashed fiercely over spheres of influence in the Caucasus. This geopolitical rivalry made use of all the means available at the time: wars between spies and diplomats, covert operations, arms smuggling, ideological battles, and active media propaganda. Read more about the confrontation between Russia and Britain, the secret operations in the Caucasus, and the lessons that those who now place their trust in Britain should draw from history.
To India via the Caucasus
“Britain will defend the freedom-loving nation from Russian aggression,” “British military advisers supplied fighters with weapons to resist the Russian army,” “British diplomats organized elites to combat Russian influence” – such headlines have become commonplace in Western media during the Ukraine conflict. Yet these same phrases could very well describe another historical conflict where British and Russian interests collided: the covert war waged by the British Empire against Russia in the 19th century, aimed at undermining Russian influence in the Caucasus.
At first glance, it might seem odd that events in the Caucasus, occurring far from Britain, could threaten London’s interests. But it only appears so.
After the Napoleonic Wars, the Russian Empire was at the height of its power. It led the “Holy Alliance” – a coalition of European great powers that shaped continental politics. Additionally, during the late 18th and early 19th centuries, Russia achieved significant victories over the Ottoman Empire in several wars, acquiring territories such as New Russia, Crimea, and parts of the eastern Black Sea coast.
Naturally, Russia also paid attention to what was happening in the Caucasus. The peoples of the North and West Caucasus, the Circassians, carried out frequent raids on Russian settlers, whom they robbed and enslaved, which caused great concern in Russia. To protect its interests and secure the safety of its people, Russia advanced further into this mountainous territory.
Britain, however, perceived this as a direct threat to its interests in India. London believed that Russia wouldn’t stop in the Caucasus but would advance further, potentially threatening Persia. And through Persia, and then Afghanistan, there lay a direct path to India, which was then referred to as the “jewel in the crown” of the British Empire. Although there was no concrete evidence that Russia intended to seize distant India, British elites firmly held this belief. In order to safeguard India against the mythical “Russian threat,” Britain encouraged tensions in the Caucasus.
In service of the Crown
Britain’s active intervention in Russian affairs in the Caucasus was preceded by two wars: the Russo-Persian War of 1826-1828 and the Russo-Turkish War of 1828-1829. As a result of these military triumphs, Russia solidified its position in Transcaucasia and gained control over much of the eastern coastline of the Black Sea.
Fearing Russia’s growing power in the region, Britain started supplying the Circassians with weapons and ammunition as early as 1830. For instance, in December of that year, six weapon-laden vessels were intercepted off the coast of what is now Abkhazia. However, for a time, these arms shipments remained limited to smuggling.
A turning point in Russia-Britain relations came with the arrival of British diplomat David Urquhart in Istanbul. A highly energetic individual, Urquhart had joined the rebels who fought for Greek independence when he was just 16 years old. After the war, he stayed in the region and developed a keen interest in the politics and culture of the Ottoman Empire. By 1833, he was appointed to the British trade delegation in Istanbul, and in 1835 he became the embassy secretary. It was Urquhart who crafted Britain’s aggressive anti-Russia policy in the Caucasus.
Urquhart initiated the work of British diplomats and spies directly in Circassia, as the Northern and Western Caucasus regions were then called. He attended elder councils and fervently promoted the idea of waging war against Russia. Notably, he was behind the adoption of a “national oath” by the mountain peoples, proposing that the Circassians unite for a common cause against Russia instead of fighting each other.
He also persuaded the Circassians to take an oath according to which anyone who entered negotiations with the Russians would be killed, their possessions divided among their executioners, and their families sold into slavery. A parallel can be drawn with contemporary Ukrainian politics, where any possibility of peacefully resolving the conflict with Russia is utterly unacceptable, and proponents of such initiatives face severe repercussions.
Urquhart proved to be an effective diplomat and spy, convincing Circassian leaders that Britain genuinely sought their independence. In reality, they were merely pawns in the hands of British agents, sacrificing themselves in the name of the British Empire, which was only concerned about the illusory Russian threat in India.
Britain also supplied the highlanders with arms. British intelligence agents James Bell and James Longworth oversaw smuggling operations that delivered firearms to the Caucasus, bribing tribal leaders and elders in the region. For an extended period, they lived undercover in the Caucasus, adopting Muslim names and fictitious titles. On behalf of the British government, they promised the Circassians that Britain was committed to protecting their independence and even vowed to fight against Russia. Throughout the 1830s, dozens of British agents were active in the Caucasus.
Most importantly, Urquhart focused on a propaganda war. An ardent Russophobe, he convinced the British public that Russia posed a deadly existential threat to the British Empire. He argued that Russia was preparing to conquer Persia and further invade India. The British press played a crucial role in spreading fears of a “Russian threat.”
Newspapers reported on the struggle of the “freedom-loving highlanders” against the “barbaric Russian oppressors.” They conveniently overlooked the fact that the highlanders themselves were quite savage at the time – slave trade and blood feuds were common in the region, and the enlightened Russian Empire resolutely opposed this.
But just like in Ukraine today, the London media exaggerated the losses of the Russian Army, insisting that the decisive support of the highlanders would ensure Russia’s defeat in the Caucasus.
The ‘Vixen’ case
While Britain’s supply of weapons to the highlanders and its organizational and ideological efforts harmed Russia, this did not decisively influence the course of the conflict. British hawks opted for provocation, aiming to ignite a conflict between Russia and Britain and other Western European nations. The pretext they found was rather unusual.
Russia was defending its legitimate interests in the Caucasus and sought to halt arms shipments to the highlanders. To this end, the Russian Navy patrolled the eastern Black Sea coast, directing all foreign commercial vessels to only two ports: Anapa and Redoubt Kali (near modern-day Poti). Britain viewed this as a violation of free trade and resorted to blatant provocation.
In November 1836, Russian military brig the Ayaks detained British schooner the Vixen in the port of Sujuk-Qale (modern-day Novorossiysk). The British vessel was unloading arms intended for the highlanders: eight cannons, nearly 13 tons of gunpowder, and a large quantity of firearms. Clearly, this wasn’t about free trade; this was direct military support for Russia’s adversaries.
The expedition was organized by none other than Urquhart, while the captain of the schooner was the British spy Bell. Remarkably, Bell didn’t hide his intentions; he openly sought to provoke the Russian fleet. After the capture, the Vixen was confiscated, and its crew expelled to Türkiye.
This incident sparked a major scandal that nearly brought the Russian and British empires to the brink of war. Conservatives in the British Parliament called for the navy to be sent to the Black Sea to confront Russia and questioned the legality of annexing Circassia. However, the British radicals miscalculated.
Russian Emperor Nicholas I refused to back down. Instead, he placed the armed forces on heightened alert and demonstrated an unwavering commitment to defending Russia’s interests in the Caucasus. No one in Europe was willing to wage war against Russia either.
As a result, London had to recall Urquhart from Istanbul and abandon all its demands regarding Russian influence in the Caucasus.
Not just the Crimean War
The war in the Caucasus could have concluded as early as the late 1830s. However, the British weren’t ready to accept defeat and began preparing for another conflict.
Agitators infiltrated the eastern Caucasus, modern-day Chechnya and Dagestan, inciting the highlanders to resist Russia. British agents assured them that London would support a rebellion against Russia and provide the necessary weapons and supplies.
The strategy was based on the assumption that Russia would become bogged down in the Caucasus and unable to counter British actions elsewhere. And that’s indeed what happened. When the Crimean War broke out from 1853 to 1856, 270,000 Russian troops were stationed in the Caucasus to maintain order in the region.
Simultaneously with the onset of the Crimean War, attacks on Russian settlements intensified, led by the forces of Imam Shamil, who controlled territories in Chechnya and Dagestan. In the North Caucasus, the Circassians launched assaults on Novorossiysk and Yekaterinodar (modern-day Krasnodar). While these raids had little impact on the overall course of battles, they undoubtedly diverted the focus and resources of the Russian command.
Throughout the Crimean War, the British press frequently raised the issue of “Circassian independence.” At the Paris Conference, London also highlighted the Circassian question, demanding that Russia recognize Circassia’s independence or, at the very least, withdraw troops from the Caucasus; in exchange London would prevent the highlanders from attacking Russian territories.
Despite this diplomatic pressure, the Russian Empire successfully defended its rights in the Caucasus. The likely reason lies in the fact that after more than 20 years of fierce struggle against Russia, the highlanders didn’t achieve any considerable progress. As for Russia, even amid a brutal war with the leading European powers of the time, it managed to retain control over the Caucasus.
Last attempt
Although the Crimean War ended in defeat for the Russian Empire, its position in the Caucasus remained stable. In an attempt to undermine Russia and lay the groundwork for future operations, the British dispatched a group of insurgents to the region in 1857.
The contingent was led by Polish military officer Teofil Lapinski, who participated in the 1848 uprising and fought against the Austrians in modern-day Ukraine and Hungary. During the Crimean War, Lapinski fought against Russia while serving in the Polish Corps, which was part of the Ottoman Army.
When, after the Crimean War, it became clear that Circassia had no chance of achieving independence, Lapinski began planning a military operation in the area. His mission was financed by pro-British General Zamojski and the Circassian elites that had settled in the Ottoman Empire. The intellectual driving force behind this operation was Stratford de Redcliffe, the British ambassador in Istanbul. Leveraging his considerable influence at the Sultan’s court, he secured the support of Ottoman officials and supplied the group with arms and ammunition.
Russian envoy Apollinary Butenev managed to uncover the plot and alerted the governor of the Caucasus, Prince Baryatinsky. Nevertheless, British steamship the Kangaroo, commanded by Captain Neggs, eluded Russian cruisers, and in February 1857, the insurgents landed in Tuapse.
The core of the unit consisted of Polish soldiers, but it also included Austrian artillerymen, Hungarian mine specialists, and Turkish instructors. British agents provided organizational and intelligence support to Lapinski’s group.
The insurgent unit was bolstered by defectors from the Russian Army, primarily Poles and Ukrainians, increasing its numbers to around 800 fighters. For about a year and a half, supported by the Circassian nobility, Lapinski effectively resisted the Russian Army. He skillfully utilized the terrain and was supported by the British and Turks.
However, General Philipson, who commanded Russian forces in this part of the Caucasus, successfully recruited one of Lapinski’s associates, who relayed crucial information about Lapinski’s actions to the imperial troops. During a bold Russian naval landing in Gelendzhik, Lapinski narrowly escaped capture. Additionally, the Russians managed to cut off supply lines for weapons and reinforcements to Lapinski’s forces and, having gathered reserves, inflicted several painful defeats on the insurgents.
The situation worsened when the British realized the inevitable defeat of the Circassians and their insurgent allies and withdrew their support. By the end of 1859, Lapinski and what remained of his insurgent group retreated to Istanbul.
That same year, Russian troops captured Imam Shamil, the leader of the highland peoples of the Northeast Caucasus. Though some scattered groups continued to resist, the overall campaign was over. Hundreds of thousands of Circassians unwilling to live under Russian rule relocated to the Ottoman Empire.
By 1864, the Caucasian War concluded with Russia’s victory, solidifying its control over the region. This triumph not only marked a significant military achievement but also ushered in a lasting peace, the abolition of slavery and brutal traditions, and the beginning of civil governance, education, and economic development in the Caucasus.
It was also a triumph for Russia over Britain, which, despite all its diplomacy, intelligence efforts, and covert operations, failed to overcome the strength of Russian intelligence services, diplomacy, and army.
This serves as an important reminder to the nations and states that count on the support of Britain when waging war against Russia. While they may have some occasional success, ultimately, the outcome will always be the same.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian airbase and industrial site in overnight attacks
articles.body:
Ukraine struck targets deep inside Russia overnight into Saturday, with explosions reported near a military airbase in Nizhny Novgorod region and an industrial facility in Samara. The attacks followed a series of Ukrainian strikes on Russian military, port and energy infrastructure, including the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk.
Russian monitoring channels reported explosions and fires around Savasleyka military airbase in Nizhny Novgorod region on 15 August. The base hosts MiG-31 aircraft used by Russia to launch Kinzhal missiles against Ukraine, according to the Kyiv Independent.
The Kyiv Independent said monitoring channel Exilenova Plus reported fires near the airfield following explosions. The newspaper said the reports had not been independently verified.
Further explosions were reported in Samara, about 800km from the Ukrainian border. Samara regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed that missiles had struck an industrial facility but did not identify the site. He said authorities were assessing damage and checking for casualties.
The strikes came days after Ukraine carried out an attack on Novorossiysk, one of Russia’s main Black Sea ports.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the Novorossiysk operation as unusual because Ukrainian forces coordinated a range of weapons developed and manufactured in Ukraine. Ukraine’s General Staff also reported the use of several domestic systems.
Ukrainian outlets RBC and Dev.ua reported that the operation involved Palianytsia, Bars and Peklo missile-drone systems, Neptune missiles and nine types of lighter drones. Some of the drones targeted Russian air defences while other weapons attacked sites around the port.
Ukraine’s General Staff said five Russian naval vessels were destroyed or damaged. It identified the frigates Admiral Makarov and Admiral Essen, patrol ship Vasily Bykov, intelligence vessel Priazovye and research vessel Viktor Cherevkov.
The claims have not received independent confirmation. Ukraine struck two frigates and several other Russian naval vessels at Novorossiysk on 12 August. The attack also targeted the Sheskharis oil terminal.
Ukraine has expanded attacks on infrastructure far from the front line during 2026. Its forces have targeted oil refineries, ports, airfields and military logistics sites.
Ukraine’s General Staff said forces struck the Ust-Luga port in Russia’s Leningrad region on 14 August, damaging two processing facilities and starting a fire, according to the Kyiv Independent. A day earlier, Ukraine said it hit Gazprom’s Neftekhim Salavat refinery in Bashkortostan, about 1,300km from Ukraine.
The attacks have taken place as Russia increases its use of ballistic and hypersonic missiles against Ukrainian cities.
Ukrainian military intelligence deputy chief Vadym Skibitskyi told RBC that Russia launched 198 ballistic and hypersonic missiles in July, the highest monthly figure this year. He said Russian factories were producing more than 100 such missiles each month.
Ukraine has also reported gains on the ground. Zelenskyy claimed Ukrainian forces had retaken 745 square kilometres and 26 settlements during an operation in the southern Dnipropetrovsk region.
HT

articles.title: Don’t Expect Russians to Protest the War
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Long Shot
The country may have hoped that deeper drone attacks would cause Russians to protest the war, but mass demonstrations don’t look likely.
This summer, Ukraine began one of the most ambitious campaigns of its war with Russia. It launched drones deep into Russian territory, hitting some of the country’s biggest oil refineries and causing a nationwide fuel shortage. In some areas, Russians have waited for gas for as long as 69 hours, in lines stretching miles. Impatient drivers have beaten and stabbed one another. Even state-controlled media have acknowledged the problem.
Ukraine and its allies seemed to hope that frustrated Russians would rise up in protest. After more than four years, the war had finally “come home.” Now that more citizens were feeling its effects, one might assume, they would demand its end and apply pressure to President Vladimir Putin ahead of parliamentary elections in the fall. But so far, no mass uprising appears likely, now or anytime soon.
Russians are used to inconveniences. Under Soviet rule, they lived with shortages of just about everything. Lines were so ubiquitous that academics theorized about Russian identity being shaped by waiting. Books were published with chapter titles such as “The Queue as a Form of Soviet Life.” The newspaper Socialist Industry estimated that Soviet citizens spent 30 billion working hours a year waiting in line for essential goods.
In the late 1980s, at the peak of Soviet scarcity, my family lived on the outskirts of Gorky, a city east of Moscow. Sometimes my mother would send me shopping. I hated it. At a small, gray store called Vegetables, I would wait in line to pick through boxes of rotting produce, hoping to find an acceptable carrot or beetroot for borscht. Then I went to Bread, where I waited some more. Shelves were half empty. The only item that never seemed to run out was margarine; enterprising salespeople tried to make it more appealing by sculpting it into hedgehogs, which they put in display cases. Lines got even longer on the rare days when cheese or butter were delivered. Meat hardly ever came.
Still, nobody protested. We waved away the deprivation and delays. Everyone lives this way, we told ourselves. After all, Soviets knew the cost of complaining. In 1962, thousands of demonstrators gathered to protest wage cuts and government-imposed price increases. In response, Premier Nikita Khrushchev’s government deployed thousands of troops, who killed roughly two dozen demonstrators in what became known as the Novocherkassk massacre.
Russians continue to fear their government. I recently called my former neighbor in St. Petersburg, an art teacher and activist whom I’ll call Svetlana. When I asked whether she had witnessed any street protests, she laughed. “Are you guys living on the moon out there?” she asked me. “Don’t you get how dangerous it is here?”
“It’s even worse than in the Soviet days,” Svetlana continued. “One guy bragged to me the other day that he’d reported his neighbor to the FSB”—the successor of the KGB—simply for listening to anti-war music. She also told me about an acquaintance who had spent two years in prison for leaving a poem and flowers at a monument to a Ukrainian poet. In most households, gripes about the regime don’t leave the kitchen.
At the start of the war, demonstrations were more common. In 2022, police arrested nearly 19,000 anti-war activists, according to OVD-Info, an independent human-rights group. Since then, protests have all but disappeared. This year, one of the most notable critics of the regime was a veteran named Alexander Lunin. In June, Lunin put on his military uniform and recorded a speech denouncing Putin and the war. He posted it on social media, where it received more than 12 million views in 24 hours. The police jailed him, and Lunin publicly apologized for “giving in to emotions due to fatigue.”
Earlier this week, the only anti-war party was banned from parliamentary elections. Far-right politicians had sued the party, named Yabloko, alleging that it had received foreign funding, violated copyright law, and promoted “extremism.” The supreme court ruled in the far right’s favor, removing Yabloko from the ballot. Only a few hundred Russians protested outside the court.
Most Russians seem to have inherited the long-suffering mentality of the generations who grew up under Soviet rule. Rather than tiring of the war, “Russians realize that they are under attack, and that it’s time to stand together and tighten their belts,” Irina Borogan, a journalist who has studied Russian dissidents, told me. When the BBC asked a middle-aged man living in Crimea about the fuel shortages, he shrugged them off: “We are humans. We’ll adapt.”
Last month, I called Konstantin Sonin, an economist and a professor at the University of Chicago who left Russia in 2015. He told me that his friends in Moscow have made only the barest wartime accommodations—such as sending their kids to summer camp in Gelendzhik, a town on the Black Sea coast, instead of one in the heavily shelled Crimea, even though both areas are well within range of Ukrainian drones. He sounded astonished by his friends’ comfort with risk. “We’ve seen what Ukrainians have been capable of coping with,” Sonin told me. “Russians can endlessly adapt to this crisis too.”
I heard a similar message from Vladislav Inozemtsev, a Russian economist and political scientist who lives in the United States. Inozemtsev told me that his friends in Moscow have used their contacts to circumvent the fuel shortage and get gas delivered to their door. “It’s twice the normal price, but they can afford it; the middle class quickly adapts to difficulties,” he said, while acknowledging that Russians in rural areas will likely have a harder time.
By some accounts, Moscow hardly looks like the capital of a country fighting a war of attrition. Denis Volkov, the director of the Levada Center, an independent polling organization, described his walk to work to me. The city center, he told me, is filled with decorations that the government has put up: an oversized samovar, an inflatable elephant, sprawling flower beds. Volkov said that he sees no sign of a public revolt. “I would say that the expectations of a revolution in Russia are not based on any real facts,” he said. “All our data proves the opposite.”
A few months before the war, Levada found that Putin’s approval rating was 63 percent. In June, it was 74 percent, although it has been dropping since the start of the year. A majority of Russians—52 percent—said that their country was moving in the right direction. “People blame mainly the West and Washington for all their troubles” instead of Putin, Volkov said. These findings undoubtedly reflect the reluctance of citizens in an authoritarian country to complain to pollsters about their government. Nonetheless, according to Volkov, Levada found that 16 percent of Russians said that they would participate in street protests, up from 11 percent in 2024. Last year, 16 percent of respondents said they felt fear or sadness. This summer, that figure was 29 percent.
Even though there have been no signs of mass protest, Putin is preparing. This year, the Kremlin increased the budget for the national guard and other law-enforcement agencies to a record high of more than $47 billion. Just like Russians who fear the reprise of Soviet-era government violence, Putin also has a precedent to worry about. In 1991, after years of keeping Russians off the streets, the Soviet regime was unable to stop a rally of hundreds of thousands in Moscow, which accelerated its end. Putin may not have much reason to fear such a protest in the near future, but he can’t be too careful.

articles.title: Seoul called for dialogue with North Korea on formally ending Korean War
articles.body:
Seoul called for dialogue with North Korea on formally ending Korean War
Kyiv • UNN
Lee Jae-myung called for talks with North Korea, proposing to replace the armistice with a peace regime. He also emphasized the need to prevent conflict and limit Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung called for the resumption of dialogue with North Korea to ensure peaceful coexistence and prevent a new conflict on the Korean Peninsula. The Guardian writes, UNN reports.
Details
"South Korean President Lee Jae-myung called for talks with North Korea aimed at achieving peaceful coexistence, stating that Seoul would seek guarantees to prevent conflict and emphasizing the need to replace the armistice on the peninsula with a 'peace regime,'" the publication writes.
In a speech marking the anniversary of Korea's liberation from Japanese colonial rule, Lee said that the two Koreas should hold talks aimed at coexistence.
He called for dialogue between North Korea and interested parties with the aim of ending the 1950–1953 Korean War, which was halted not by a peace treaty but by an armistice, and noted that measures to limit Pyongyang's nuclear capabilities could also be considered during the discussions.
Lee also said that Seoul would take preventive and consistent measures to ease tensions and create multilayered safeguards to prevent an escalation of the conflict.
As the publication notes, Lee's call is largely based on his pledge last year to respect North Korea's system and seek peaceful coexistence with Pyongyang.
DPRK removes references to unification with South Korea from constitution06.05.26, 11:17 • 4751 view
As the publication points out, relations between North and South Korea remain frozen. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un abandoned Pyongyang's policy of reunification, called South Korea the most hostile state, and ordered the strengthening of defenses along the front line.
North Korea rejected Lee's proposals to establish dialogue, criticized Seoul's plan for nuclear-powered submarines, and condemned joint U.S.–South Korean military exercises as provocations.
Regarding relations with Japan, Lee called for confronting the past while leaving the future open, and expressed hope of beginning a new 60 years of peace and prosperity with Japan as a "close neighbor."
To remind you
On the morning of August 12, North Korea launched a ballistic missile toward the sea, conducting its second missile test in less than a week.

articles.title: Ukraine attacks Russian air base and rocket plant in Samara region
articles.body:
Ukraine attacks Russian air base and rocket plant in Samara region
Ukraine struck industrial infrastructure in Russia's Samara region on Saturday, local authorities said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the attack, saying a rocket plant and air base were hit.
A large-scale Ukrainian attack struck industrial infrastructure in Russia’s southwestern Samara region Saturday, a Russian official said.
Ivan Noskov, head of the region's capital, Samara, said air defence forces had repelled a “massive” missile attack, with “localised damage” to the city’s industrial sites. He also said that medical assistance has been provided to those injured in the attack, but did not give further details.
Ukraine has stepped up its long-range aerial attacks on Russian military industries and energy facilities, aiming to cut Moscow’s revenue for the war and make Russians feel the consequences of the invasion, now in its fifth year.
Read moreFast and fearless: Baltic defence startups innovate to counter Russian threat
Writing on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Kyiv’s forces had carried out a strike against Samara’s Progress Center, which operates under Russian space agency Roscosmos and is involved in producing rocket technology and electronics.
He said that the strike used Ukraine’s domestically produced Flamingo missiles to hit the site, which is approximately 900 kilometres (560 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Zelensky also said Russia's Savasleyka air base, some 700 kilometres (430 miles) from the front line, had also been hit.
“Peace is needed, and this must be evident in Russia – through concrete damage to specific facilities,” Zelensky wrote.
While most of Ukraine’s strikes have a range of less than 200 kilometres (125 miles), its longer-range attacks have increased dramatically this year. It launched three times as many of those strikes in July as it did in January, according to data from ACLED, an independent conflict monitor. Repeatedly hitting deep into Russia has forced its military to stretch air defences over a larger area.
Read moreHundreds of Ukrainian drones target Russia in deadly overnight strikes
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said Saturday that it had shot down 598 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions, as well as the Black and Azov Seas and the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea.
Separately, two people, including a nine-year-old child, were wounded when a Ukrainian drone attack hit a private home in the town of Shatura in the Moscow region, local Gov. Andrey Vorobyov said.
Elsewhere, a Russian strike on an apartment block in southeastern Ukraine Saturday killed a three-month-old baby and wounded 11 people, local officials said.
Drones hit the building in the town of Marhanets, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration.
Russia's Ministry of Defence also said that it had targeted warehouses and infrastructure at the Ukrainian ports of Odesa, Izmail and Yuzhnyi.
Ukraine’s Air Force said that Russia launched 152 drones over the country Saturday, of which 124 were destroyed.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

articles.title: Ukraine’s quiet counteroffensive took 745 square km. Russia’s dead Starlink is how
articles.body:
- In six months of unheralded advances, Ukrainian forces liberated a wide stretch of the southeast
- The collapse of Russian communications turned a local push into a six-month advance
- Now the Russians may mobilize yet again, so the Ukrainians are digging in and consolidating their gains
The scale of Ukrainian forces' counteroffensive in southeastern Ukraine early this year is finally becoming clear. In six months of maneuver starting on 29 January, a clutch of Ukrainian units, including the 78th, 79th, 80th, 82nd, and 95th Air Assault Brigades and the 1st and 425th Assault Regiments—tens of thousands of troops, in all—marched through gaps in Russian defenses and, according to Ukrainian officials, liberated around 745 square km and 26 settlements. Mostly in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast but also in neighboring Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk Oblasts.
That is Kyiv's own accounting, and it is the high end. The Institute for the Study of War, which maps control from geolocated imagery, put the figure at roughly 627 square km across the Oleksandrivka direction and the northern Hulyaipole direction—while noting its own conservative method probably undercounts. Either number describes the largest Ukrainian territorial gain since 2023.
The Ukrainian gains helped to offset Russian gains around the last few free cities in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast. Between the start of February and the end of July, Russian regiments captured a net total of just 260 square km of Ukrainian soil, according to a tally by the Black Bird Group. It would've been more than 1,000 square km if those air assault and assault units hadn't been busy clearing the Russians from a wide swathe of the southeast.
The Ukrainian counteroffensive kicked off on 29 January. Three days later, Elon Musk's Starlink bricked Russia's thousands of smuggled and stolen satellite terminals. Practically overnight, the Russians lost their best method for controlling small drones and guiding assault units across the disputed gray zone. Drones couldn't fly. Troops couldn't navigate.
Ukrainian commanders surely knew their communications advantage wouldn't last: the Russians would eventually adapt with new methods of command and control. Seizing the opportunity, Ukrainian paratroopers and assault troops pressed the attack. And in stark contrast to the usual assault tactics for both sides, the Ukrainians attacked in tanks and other armored vehicles, counting on the Russians' connectivity problems to clear a path for heavy forces.
The blackout was not the only thing working in Ukraine's favor. ISW credits the gains to five reinforcing factors: better operational planning, a campaign to suppress and destroy Russian air defenses, deeper strikes on Russian logistics, Ukrainian drone superiority at the tactical level—and the Starlink cutoff. But the cutoff is the one that arrived all at once, and it arrived just as Ukrainian armor was starting to move.
Mechanized assaults
Not all the vehicles got through. The assault troops lost one up-armored M-1 Abrams tank in early February. But by March, other assault forces M-1s were engaging Russian troops at point-blank range with their 120-mm main guns. After clearing a few disputed villages along a 45-km front between Dobropillya and Zelenyi Hai, the Ukrainians focused their maneuver and firepower on Komar, 12 km southeast of Zelenyi Hai.
The Ukrainians "started a slow and quiet offensive, with very few videos and small teams, during April and May," mapper Clément Molin recalled. The strict information security obscured the Ukrainian moves for all but the closest observers, allowing Ukrainian commanders to press their attacks without drawing too much attention—and risking a Russian countercounteroffensive.
By summer, the Ukrainians were within mortar range of Komar. Embarrassed Russian commanders resorted to sending out small teams on virtual suicide missions to plant Russian flags in disputed territory. The flags could create the impression of Russian control on terrain that, in fact, neither side controlled. "Russia is trying to intoxicate us with flag videos, which are meant to hide the real situation to both us and their command," Molin wrote.
The reality was that the Ukrainians had gained ground. A lot of it.
Trending Now
Announcing the results on 12 August, Ukrainian officials also claimed 9,550 Russian troops killed and more than 6,600 wounded—figures no independent body has verified. Former commander in chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, who planned the operation, said it proved the Ukrainian army "is capable not only of steadfastly holding its defences, but also of launching offensives, seizing the initiative, and liberating Ukrainian land."
But the momentum was unsustainable. As the Russians gradually restored command and control through the summer, the Ukrainians encountered more resistance. Now the gray zone is stabilizing again. Observer Moklasen predicted new Ukrainian commander in chief Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi will order his corps and brigade commanders "to dig in positions, consolidate and strengthen more army corps" instead of continuing to attack.
After all, the Russians are pushing hard in Donetsk, and the resources the Ukrainians had devoted to the southeastern counteroffensive could boost the defensive effort in the east. Moreover, there are worrying signs the Kremlin may attempt another mobilization soon, potentially surging hundreds of thousands of fresh troops into Ukraine.
The Ukrainians may soon prioritize holding over attacking.

articles.title: More than 100 drones detected near Romania in four days, NATO jets scrambled seven times
articles.body:
More than 100 drones were detected near Romania over the past 96 hours, with NATO fighter jets scrambled seven times in response to the increased aerial activity, Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruță said, according to Antena 3 CNN.
The figures come as Romania faces a growing number of drone incidents linked to Russia’s war against Ukraine. Romanian forces have recently shifted from monitoring and escorting drones to actively destroying those that enter Romanian airspace, while NATO aircraft are increasingly being called on to respond to aerial threats along the alliance’s eastern flank.
NATO aircraft repeatedly activated
According to Miruță, Romanian authorities detected more than 100 drones in the vicinity of Romanian territory during the four-day period. NATO fighter jets participating in air-policing missions were activated seven times.
Miruță did not report how many of the detected drones entered Romanian airspace, nor how many were identified as Russian or Ukrainian.
Miruță said most of the drones were destroyed by Ukrainian air defenses outside Romania, but close enough for their debris to reach Romanian shores.
“[Russia’s war in Ukraine] is a real war, with real consequences. That is why we are taking every measure we can to limit the indirect consequences that are also being felt here,” Miruță wrote on Facebook.
The report comes shortly after Romania destroyed two Russian Gerbera-type drones that were found drifting in the Black Sea near the Neptun Deep offshore gas project on 11 August. Romanian military divers carried out controlled detonations after Ukraine confirmed the drones were not Ukrainian.
Romania has begun shooting down drones
The latest figures follow a significant change in Romania’s response to drone incursions.
In late July, Romanian F-16s shot down three drones over Romanian territory and territorial waters in three consecutive days. One of the drones was identified as a Russian Shahed-type attack drone, while investigations were conducted into the others.
The July incidents marked a shift from Romania’s previous approach of tracking or escorting drones that crossed into its airspace during Russian attacks on Ukraine. Four of the five drones shot down in EU and NATO countries at that point had been neutralized by Romanian military pilots, according to Miruță.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan called the repeated violations of Romanian airspace “inadmissible and intolerable” and Bucharest prepared a diplomatic protest to Moscow after one of the downed drones was identified as Russian.
Drone war reaches beyond Ukraine
Romania has repeatedly dealt with drones crossing its border during Russian attacks on Ukrainian territory, particularly in the vicinity of Ukrainian ports on the Danube and the Black Sea.
In June, a Ukrainian sea drone that had lost control, which Kyiv attributed to Russian electronic warfare, exploded near an oil terminal in the Romanian port of Constanța. No one was injured, but more than 1,000 people were evacuated from the area as a precaution.
The incidents have also extended beyond Romania. On 14 August, NATO fighter jets shot down a foreign drone after it entered Latvian airspace. Latvia said the drone had entered its airspace as a result of Russian electronic warfare activity.
The repeated incidents have made drone activity around NATO’s eastern border an increasingly regular consequence of Russia’s war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukrainian missiles attack Russian region – governor
articles.body:
Ukrainian missiles attack Russian region – governor
An industrial facility in Russia’s Samara Region was attacked by Ukrainian missiles, local governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said.
Emergency services have been deployed on site, Fedorishchev wrote in a Saturday morning post on Max.
The information regarding damage and casualties is currently being verified, he added.
In the Rostov Region, around 1,000 residents of seven villages were left without electricity after a Ukrainian drone damaged powerlines in the area, according to local governor Yury Slusar.
Around a dozen UAVs and three missiles were destroyed by air defenses in the region overnight, Slusar said. There have been no reports of injuries, he added.
Ukraine has several types of long-range missiles in their arsenal, including British-supplied Storm Shadow and homemade Flamingo munitions.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin wrote on Max that at least 16 incoming drones were shot down on the approach to the Russian capital during the night.
In the town of Shatura in Moscow Region, a UAV hit a private home, injuring a 9-year-old boy and a 55-year-old woman, local governor Vyacheslav Vorobyeb wrote on Telegram. The child was hospitalized in serious condition, he added.
The Russian Defense Ministry said that a total of 598 Ukrainian UAVs were shot down or intercepted by electronic warfare means above 20 of the country's regions overnight.
Moscow has condemned Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia’s civilian infrastructure and residential areas as terrorist attacks aimed at compensating for Kiev’s setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces continue their steady advance.
Russia has responded by intensifying long-range missile and drone strikes against Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities and logistics infrastructure. Moscow maintains that it does not target civilians and that its strikes are directed solely at military targets and infrastructure supporting Kiev’s forces.
The Defense Ministry in Moscow said on Friday that a total of 14 such strikes had been launched over the previous week, hitting drone production plants, weapons, and logistics centers, as well as fuel, energy, and transport infrastructure. Military airfields and ports where cargo used by Kiev’s troops are unloaded and stored have also been targeted.
The Russian military also struck 15 oceangoing vessels operating in the interests of the Ukrainian military, including a tanker, seven dry cargo ships, two tugboats, and five patrol boats, it added.

articles.title: Europe’s race for dual-use technology has a new contender: Vilnius
articles.body:
Europe’s rapid expansion of dual-use technologies is creating a new generation of innovation centers, and Vilnius is quickly becoming one of them. With strengths spanning lasers, AI, autonomous systems, and secure communications, Lithuania’s capital is building an ecosystem where research moves quickly into real-world civilian and defense applications.
From aerial drones to cybersecurity tools, technologies designed for both civilian and military use have seen increased investment and rapid development in Europe lately. Investment in these “dual-use” technologies increased 25 percent between 2024 and 2025, reaching nearly $1.2 trillion, while over 2,300 new dual-use startups launched across NATO allies in the same period. Supporting a wide range of sectors, from transport and energy to defense and communications, dual-use tech is increasingly important to Europe’s security, infrastructure, and economic interests.
In this climate, emerging tech hubs like Vilnius are establishing themselves as centers for developing and testing versatile technologies like autonomous vehicles and secure communications systems. Such initiatives lay promising foundations for the economic, employment, and security outlook of Lithuania and the wider region.
Turning research into practical dual-use solutions
In recent years, Lithuania has moved from a rich but fragmented innovation ecosystem to a tight-knit network of coordinated efforts, focused on scaling up dual-use tech with real-world applications. The capital’s well-established network of university research groups, technology startups, and defense-focused SMEs is working together, fueled by increased investment, to turn technical know-how and academic research into practical solutions for both civil and military challenges.
“Europe’s security increasingly depends on technologies that can move seamlessly between civilian and defense applications. Vilnius has the rare combination of engineering talent, advanced research, and a collaborative ecosystem that allows those technologies to be developed, tested, and deployed much faster than in larger markets,” says Artūras Medeišis, Dean of the Faculty of Electronics at VILNIUS TECH, one of Lithuania’s largest research universities for engineering, technology, and business. “The future of defense innovation won’t be built only inside defense companies. It will come from universities, startups, and deep-tech businesses working together. That’s exactly the ecosystem Vilnius has been building.”
“Dual-use technologies are no longer a niche sector; they’re becoming part of Europe’s industrial future,” says Mangirdas Šapranauskas, Head of Business at Go Vilnius, the city’s official tourism and business development agency. “Vilnius is already home to globally competitive companies developing technologies with both civilian and defense applications – from Brolis Semiconductors and Astrolight in photonics to Granta Autonomy and RSI Europe in autonomous and counter-drone systems. Combined with close collaboration between universities, startups, manufacturers and the public sector, this creates an ecosystem where innovation moves quickly from research to deployment and attracts international investment and strategic partnerships.”
Many of Lithuania’s most active dual-use areas feature technologies in high global demand. This includes lasers and photonics, cybersecurity, small satellites, wireless communications, electro-optical systems, drones, counter-drone solutions, and advanced data processing for AI and machine learning.
These tools have essential civilian functions, in everything from environmental monitoring and infrastructure inspections to supporting energy grids and government networks. But these same technologies also have important defense functions, especially for countries that face the threat of disruption to electronic systems and key infrastructure. “For countries like Lithuania, systems must remain functional under constant risk of electronic warfare, GNSS disruption, cyberattack, or infrastructure degradation,” says Medeišis. “This means that future systems must be modular, repairable, locally adaptable, and suitable for fast improvement cycles.”
Building autonomous systems at Vilnius Tech
One major step forward for Vilnius in this area is the creation of the Competence Center for Autonomous, Remotely Operated and Connected Systems (ComARC), led by VILNIUS TECH, with Kaunas University of Technology as the Lithuanian partner and Fraunhofer FKIE in Germany as the international partner. Supported by an 8 million-euro investment, the center will focus on developing technologies such as drones, ground vehicles, maritime systems, and secure communications. Core areas of development will include AI-powered sensing, autonomous navigation, drone swarm management, and specialized microelectronics for tasks such as aerial surveillance, ground logistics, and infrastructure monitoring.
“ComARC is needed now because the security environment has changed. Autonomy, drones, AI, resilient communications, and critical-infrastructure protection are no longer future topics; they are immediate strategic requirements. Lithuania cannot rely only on buying foreign technologies. It must be able to understand, test, adapt, improve, and create such systems locally,” says Artūras Medeišis.
The center is designed to grow alongside new technology and talent needs. Its plans include expanding its team to about 50 researchers, engineers, and technologists across electronics, AI, telecommunications, robotics, and materials. The center will support hands-on field testing of systems such as drones and unmanned vehicles across several Lithuanian cities, using a shared testing platform. By bringing research, industrial prototyping, and field implementation together in one location, the center will build the capacity to quickly turn experimental ideas into working prototypes and products ready to address real-world challenges.
The next generation of European innovation won’t be defined only by the biggest economies. It will be shaped by places that can quickly turn research into real-world solutions. Vilnius has built exactly that kind of ecosystem, bringing together talent, industry, and public partners to develop technologies that strengthen both economic competitiveness and resilience.
Source: govilnius.lt

articles.title: Blogger Kyivstoner May Have Been Targeted by Russian Agent in Poland Due to Preparations for New Operation Spiderweb
articles.body:
Ukrainian rapper and blogger Albert Vasilyev, known as Kyivstoner, may have been the target of an assassination plot orchestrated by Russian intelligence services in Poland.
This was reported by the Polish media outlet RMF FM, citing its own sources.
Earlier, it was reported that a Russian national recruited by Russian intelligence services was detained on August 7, thwarting an assassination attempt on a U.S. and Ukrainian citizen in Warsaw.
The identity of the potential victim was not disclosed, but Tusk clarified that this person was targeted because they posed a threat to Putin’s regime.
And today, August 14, RMF FM reported that the individual in question may be Albert Vasilyev.
The FSB accused Vasilyev of allegedly organizing the logistics for delivering drones to the Moscow region.
According to the FSB, the drones were transported through Slovakia, Poland, and Belarus for subsequent attacks on strategic facilities near Moscow. Thirty-five FPV drones for these operations were delivered to Russia disguised as a shipment of Spanish ceramic tiles via a route through Slovakia, Poland, and Belarus. The FSB also claimed that the drones were to be launched from a rented hangar near the facility.
Following this, Russian authorities added the musician to a list of individuals they consider to be involved in terrorist and extremist activities.
This may have been one of the reasons why Russian intelligence agencies viewed him as a target, particularly in light of preparations for a new operation based on the scenario of Operation Spiderweb.
Vasilyev himself denied all these allegations.
The suspect was detained in Warsaw by police officers in cooperation with the Polish Internal Security Agency (ABW).
According to RMF FM, the suspect was born in Ukraine, although Poland’s Minister-Coordinator of Special Services, Tomasz Semoniak, stated that the detainee was of Russian origin.
Albert Vasilyev rose to fame as a blogger and later became one of the founders of the Ukrainian band Hryby. After leaving the band, he continued his musical career under the pseudonym Kyivstoner.
At the same time, Polish law enforcement agencies have not officially named the person who may have been the target of the planned assassination. Therefore, the information that it was Kyivstoner is currently based on reports from Polish media outlets citing their own sources.
