Ukraine Blows Up Russian Missile and Artillery Depot in Occupied Crimea, Video
Ukrainian forces destroyed a Russian missile and artillery ammunition depot near Solone Ozero in temporarily occupied Crimea in a joint drone operation involving the 422nd Unmanned Systems Regiment and the Security Service of Ukraine’s Alpha special operations unit.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on August 15, the strike targeted a Russian military facility near Solone Ozero, northeast of Dzhankoi. The operation was supported by the 3rd Department of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
Footage of the attack was published by Mykola Kolesnyk, commander of the 422nd Unmanned Systems Regiment. Militarnyi and OSINT analyst blinzka subsequently geolocated the site and identified it as a missile and artillery storage facility near the settlement.
Satellite fire-monitoring data from NASA FIRMS recorded a large fire at the location on August 13. Open-source mapping data also indicates the presence of a Russian military facility in the area, according to Militarnyi.
Ukrainian forces used domestically produced medium-range strike drones during the operation, including the Ukrainian-made Zozulia unmanned aerial vehicle.
Ukraine has continued targeting Russian air-defense and drone infrastructure across occupied Crimea. On August 10, HUR reported that its Group 13 unit destroyed two Russian S-400 launchers and an antenna used to control Orion reconnaissance-and-strike drones, using Magura naval platforms carrying FPV drones.

articles.title: Vance Says Keeping Oil Prices Low Is US ‘Goal Number 1’ in Iran War
articles.body:
US Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that the top US priority in the Iran war is keeping oil and gasoline prices low for Americans, while preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon ranks second.
The remarks contrast with US President Donald Trump’s repeated framing of the fight: that entering the war had the sole objective of preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, even if that meant short-term economic sacrifices for Americans.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Vance’s comments also underscore the growing reality that the war now centers on control of the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has forced to the top of the negotiating agenda.
“I know that oil is down today and it’s way down from the highs in the early days of the conflict,” Vance said on Fox News. “That’s goal number one – keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country.”
“And then obviously goal number two is ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon,” he added.
The vice president has been among the members of the administration most skeptical of the offensive launched against Iran in late February.
His latest remarks, however, appear to confirm the more cautious approach now favored by the US president, which involves maintaining strong economic pressure on Iran while a military standoff in the Strait of Hormuz persists.
“Sometimes we’re focused on the energy piece of it because we want Americans to be able to afford the price of oil and gas. Sometimes we’re obviously focused on the military... on the nuclear program,” Vance also said.
‘Patriot Licenses for Ukraine are Not in America’s Interest’ | Stefan Korshak
Vance added that Trump was “at the height of his authority with a lot of tools – diplomatic, military and economic.”
The decision to focus on economic pressure comes as the diplomatic path appears blocked, with both Washington and Tehran sticking to their conditions for reopening the strait.
Regarding his military options, US media report that Trump must contend with rapid depletion of stocks of certain missiles and drones.

articles.title: Russia hunted civilians by drone in Kherson. Victims are suing the US firm they say helped connect the attackers
articles.body:
A New York networking company sold radios that let signals travel 100 kilometers. Ukrainian civilians say Russian drone crews used them to hunt people in Kherson, and they are asking a Manhattan jury to hold the company responsible.
Ukrainian civilians and relatives of people killed by Russian drones sued Ubiquiti Inc. in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York on 11 August, alleging the company's wireless equipment became the backbone of the command network behind Russia's "human safari" against civilians.
The case rests on a comparison that the plaintiffs draw themselves. In February 2026, Starlink terminals that Russian forces had mounted on reconnaissance and strike drones were shut off after Ukraine and SpaceX built a whitelist of authorized terminals. Ubiquiti, the complaint alleges, had the same technical and contractual power over its own devices and did not use it.
That precedent cuts both ways. SpaceX had denied for years that Russian forces were using Starlink systematically, and the whitelist came together only after Ukraine's newly appointed defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, approached the company directly. The fix was technically possible—and it took a government to force it.
What the lawsuit claims
The law firm DiCello Levitt LLP filed the case, Kovalenko et al. v. Ubiquiti, Inc., No. 1:26-cv-06838. The plaintiffs are Ukrainian civilians who were maimed, displaced, or forced to live under drone surveillance, along with family members of civilians killed in drone attacks. They are seeking a jury trial.
Ubiquiti, listed on the New York Stock Exchange as UI, makes long-range wireless "bridges" widely used for internet access in areas without cable. Its radio bridge antennas and airMAX technology are subject to US export restrictions on Russia. The complaint alleges the devices kept reaching Russian forces through intermediary supply chains, and that they now link reconnaissance units, drone operators, attack units, and commanders across roughly 100 kilometers of encrypted battlefield network.
"Battlefield communications are the central nervous system of the Russian occupation forces: without them, they could not coordinate the human safari or maintain the occupation," Scott Gilmore, the lead attorney for the plaintiffs and a partner at DiCello Levitt, said in an interview with Euromaidan Press.
The complaint cites US export-control restrictions, Russian import data, public reporting, Russian military statements, battlefield images and video, and Ubiquiti's own device telemetry. It alleges the company held location data showing where its devices were operating, including inside Russia and occupied Ukrainian territory, and that it was repeatedly warned its products were being smuggled across the border.
It further alleges Ubiquiti continued issuing firmware updates and technical support that kept those devices running, and that it could have cut the pipeline off—by geofencing, by terminating distributors tied to sanctions-evasion routes, or by building a remote-disable feature into its firmware.
"Companies cannot willfully blind themselves when sanctions and export controls are being breached, and their devices are being foreseeably used in dangerous ways," Gilmore said. "US law is clear that companies bear legal responsibility when they entrust dangerous devices to end users who they know or should know are hurting people. This case is not about standard warfare: it's about murdering civilians."
The plaintiffs bring eight causes of action, including negligent entrustment, public nuisance, strict products liability for design defect, negligent product design, negligent infliction of emotional distress, and aiding and abetting assault, battery, and intentional infliction of emotional distress.
How the radios got to the front
The lawsuit follows an investigation published in January 2026 by Hunterbrook Media, which documented widespread use of Ubiquiti products by Russian forces. One Ukrainian communications officer told the outlet that an estimated 80% of the Russian bridges he had observed near the front line were Ubiquiti devices.
Analysis of trade records found the value of Ubiquiti shipments crossing into Russia rose by 66% after the full-scale invasion, despite US and EU export controls, and that the shipments included models released after the bans took effect. The goods moved mainly through distributors in third countries such as Kazakhstan and Türkiye. Russian units often received the bridges from volunteers who bought them with crowdfunded money.
Ubiquiti has been here before. In 2014, the company paid a $504,225 settlement to the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control after its products were delivered to Iran in violation of US sanctions between 2008 and 2011.
The campaign at the center of the case
Russia's "human safari" is a campaign in which small drones hunt and attack civilians, concentrated in Kherson and other front-line areas. Operators use drone cameras to track people, vehicles, and rescuers, and sometimes strike the same target twice.
UN investigators concluded in September 2025 that Russian short-range drone attacks on civilians along the west bank of the Dnipro River amount to the crimes against humanity of murder and forcible transfer of population. The finding covers more than 300 kilometers across Kherson, Dnipropetrovsk, and Mykolaiv oblasts. The complaint cites it as evidence.
Ukraine's Security Service has since charged 10 operators from Russia's 404th Motorized Rifle Regiment with war crimes in absentia, in a case that included explosives dropped on ambulances at a city hospital and a double strike on rescuers.
The incidents in the complaint include a married couple attacked in their car, a firefighter hunted and wounded by a drone while responding to a colleague, and an energy worker killed in a double-tap strike as colleagues tried to reach him.
Trending Now
"The human safari is one of the most horrific crimes against humanity of the 21st Century," Gilmore said. "We intend to present evidence of the widespread and systematic nature of this campaign in court, including international documentation. These coordinated attacks do not happen randomly: they require communications systems and a chain of command. That is precisely why the United States banned the export of Ubiquiti's radio bridge antennas to Russia—because they are necessary for Russia's war machine."
Russian state media has shown the equipment in use.
Zvezda, the television channel run by Russia's Defense Ministry, aired footage on 3 July 2025 of a Ubiquiti UISP Litebeam 5AC device; a TASS report in October 2025 showed a serviceman logging into Ubiquiti's airOS operating system, and a Rossiya-1 segment that month showed one climbing a tower to mount an antenna carrying the company's logo.
A Russian seller supplied Hunterbrook with letters she said came from Russian military units, thanking her for wireless bridges they described as necessary for connections over long distances.
Ubiquiti has said nothing
Ubiquiti did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.
Neither the company nor its chief executive, Robert Pera, has publicly commented on the January investigation, according to the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. No US or EU authority has announced an enforcement action against Ubiquiti over Russia, and the company has not been formally accused of sanctions violations tied to Ukraine. The allegations in the complaint are untested, and Ubiquiti has not yet filed a response.
Inside Human Safari: the film that captures Russia’s drones hunting Ukrainians like prey
What the case would establish
If it survives, the suit would test whether ordinary US product-liability law reaches a manufacturer whose equipment ends up in a documented atrocity—a theory that does not require proving the company intended any of it, only that it knew or should have known and failed to act.
"The question is this: what would a reasonable company do if it learned its devices were being used to coordinate murder?" Gilmore said. "If it fails to follow reasonable safety measures, shouldn't it be held liable to the civilians who get hurt? Those are the questions we intend to put before a New York jury."
Gilmore, who has investigated war crimes for two decades, said the legal framework needed already exists at national and international levels, and that in mass-atrocity cases from Syria to Sudan, investigations, jurisdiction, and remedies take years. He said he expects accountability for Ukrainian victims to come through criminal prosecutions, civil litigation, and regulatory enforcement together.
"Our clients want to shine a light on the atrocities being committed against civilians in Ukraine and to remind companies that compliance with sanctions and export controls is not a mere technicality: it's a matter of life or death," he said.
"We are at the tip of the spear."
Editor's note: Euromaidan Press correspondent Zarina Zabrisky, who conducted this interview and reports from Kherson, co-developed draft US legislation on the drone campaign—the Liability for Operators and Responsible Authorities (LORA) Act—which would impose targeted sanctions on identified drone operators, restrict exports of drone components, and require public attribution of perpetrators. She has no connection to this lawsuit or to the firm that filed it. Her documentary Kherson: Human Safari is available free at khersonhumansafari.com.

articles.title: Zelenskyy on air defence: It is not easy, but it will all happen
articles.body:
Zelenskyy on air defence: It is not easy, but it will all happen
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine is continuing efforts to strengthen its air defence and is negotiating agreements to produce the necessary weapons domestically.
Source: Zelenskyy in an evening address
Quote: "We continue working to secure air defence for Ukraine – the missiles needed to protect lives and agreements for production in Ukraine. All of this will happen. It is not easy, but all of this will happen.
Throughout the war, we have already spoken many times about weapons, capabilities, and equipment that we were initially told were supposedly impossible for us to obtain. Then we heard that Ukrainians supposedly would not be able to do it because it would take decades to become capable of it. F-16s, the production of millions of drones a year, specialised missile technologies – we did it."
Details: Zelenskyy said the same will happen with anti-ballistic capabilities and Patriot systems.
Quote: "But every delay that, unfortunately, is happening at the political level simply costs lives. It is important to act quickly, to focus all our efforts on protecting lives and limiting Russia's resources for war.
The aggressor must feel that the world is there – truly there – and is acting to end the war, rather than simply watching the war continue."
Background: Zelenskyy reported on 12 August that Ukraine had struck the Russian naval base in Novorossiysk with domestically-made Palianytsia drones and Neptun missiles.

articles.title: NATO scrambles warplanes to shoot down drone over Latvia
articles.body:
NATO scrambles warplanes to shoot down drone over Latvia
A NATO fighter jet has destroyed a drone that entered Latvian airspace, the US-led bloc has said.
The announcement came as Ukraine carried out a major UAV attack against Russia’s northwestern Leningrad Region on Friday. A total of 54 drones were shot down or intercepted above the region overnight, local governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said. A fire broke out at the key Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga during the raid, but it was swiftly extinguished, according to the governor.
There have been multiple reports in recent months of Ukrainian drones violating the airspace of Latvia, Estonia, Lithuania, and Finland, or crashing inside those countries, while on their way to Russia.
NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said on Friday that “this morning, we saw Italian Eurofighters based in Lithuania and Turkish F-16s out of Estonia scramble, with one Eurofighter downing a drone over Latvian airspace.”
The Latvian Defense Ministry also confirmed the incident, saying in a statement that “fighter jets participating in the NATO Baltic Air Policing mission successfully shot down a foreign unmanned aerial vehicle.”
The ministry claimed that the UAV “entered Latvia as a result of Russian electronic warfare activities.”
“Similar incidents involving foreign unmanned aerial vehicles entering or approaching Latvian airspace may occur” as long as the conflict between Russia and Ukraine continues, the statement added.
Last week, Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania issued a joint demarche after Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said Moscow had “verified data,” showing that Baltic states had provided air corridors for Ukrainian drones attacking Russian civilian infrastructure. The governments in Riga, Tallinn, and Vilnius denied Galuzin’s accusations as “completely unfounded.”
On Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Russian military and intelligence services “see where things fly from and how they fly,” referring to incoming UAVs.
“This is well-known to everyone, and we are not going to prove anything to anyone here,” Peskov stressed.
Moscow previously warned that if Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania knowingly help to facilitate Ukrainian drone strikes, Russia could consider them complicit in the attacks and would have the right to self-defense under the UN Charter.

articles.title: Ukraine Targets Russian Rocket Facility In Major Overnight Attack
articles.body:
Ukraine said it struck a major Russian rocket and space facility with domestically produced Flamingo cruise missiles on August 15, as Kyiv continued its campaign of long-range attacks deep inside Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram that the Progress Rocket and Space Center in Russia’s Samara region had been hit. The facility, part of Russia’s space agency Roscosmos, produces Soyuz launch vehicles.
Samara Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed that an industrial facility in the region had been hit but did not identify it. Ukrainian monitoring channels reported a fire at the Progress facility. The extent of any damage could not be independently verified.
“Today there are new significant results from our long-range strikes,” Zelenskyy said, adding that Flamingo missiles had been used and calling it “a good achievement.”
The attack on Samara came amid a wider wave of Ukrainian strikes across Russia. The country's Defense Ministry said on August 15 that its forces had intercepted 598 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight in 19 regions as well as in Russian-occupied Crimea and the Black and Azov seas. The attacks disrupted air traffic, prompting temporary restrictions at airports in several Russian cities.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine also struck the Savasleyka military airfield in the Nizhny Novgorod region, where Russian aircraft used to launch missile attacks on Ukraine are based, and an oil facility at Ust-Luga in the Leningrad region. The extent of the damage at the sites was not independently established.
“Our plan of long-range strikes against Russia in response to this war is being implemented, and it is important that Russia’s war potential continues to decrease,” Zelenskyy said.
In recent months, Ukraine has intensified long-range attacks on military and energy infrastructure inside Russia, a campaign Zelenskyy has described as Kyiv’s “long-range sanctions” against Moscow aimed at pushing the Kremlin into negotiations.
Russian authorities reported other attacks on August 15, including one that damaged power infrastructure in the Rostov region. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 15 drones heading toward the capital were shot down. In the Moscow region, authorities said falling drone debris struck a house, injuring a woman and a nine-year-old boy.
Russia, meanwhile, launched 152 attack drones at Ukraine overnight, according to the Ukrainian Air Force, which said 124 were shot down or otherwise neutralized.
Local authorities said a Russian drone killed a three-month-old child and injured 11 people in Marhanets in the Dnipropetrovsk region. Russian attacks also damaged industrial and civilian infrastructure in the Odesa and Poltava regions.
The attacks come amid a sharp rise in civilian casualties in Ukraine. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in the country said 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in July, making it the deadliest month for civilians since May 2022.
The conflict has also intensified in and around the Black Sea in recent weeks, with both sides targeting ports, vessels and other maritime infrastructure.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on August 14 rejected Ukrainian and Turkish calls for a pause in Black Sea attacks and ruled out reviving the UN- and Turkey-brokered Black Sea Grain Initiative, which had allowed Ukraine to export grain safely before Moscow withdrew in 2023.
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, signed a decree imposing sanctions on 13 vessels, 11 Russian citizens, and 28 companies that Ukrainian authorities accuse of involvement in exporting grain from Russian-occupied territory.

NATO Plans Thousands of AI Drones Along Russia and Belarus Borders
NATO is planning to strengthen its eastern flank with a network of thousands of drones, sensors, and satellites linked through artificial intelligence, according to Politico on August 14.
The system is being developed under the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative (EFDI) and is intended to monitor threats along NATO’s borders with Russia and Belarus, stretching from northern Finland to the Black Sea.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
NATO plans for the network to detect violations of allied airspace and borders and serve as the first line of defense.
The system would combine data from multiple sources in real time. For example, if a drone detects a hostile UAV, AI could compare that information with satellite images, sensor readings, and radar data before sending the information to NATO allies.
Commanders would then be able to choose which forces should respond. NATO refers to the concept as a “kill web,” designed to send information directly to operators instead of moving it through multiple levels of command.
“Previously, information went through many intermediaries. Today, it can come directly from a sensor to a tool of influence,” US Army Captain Ronan Sefton said.
The platform is being developed in Wiesbaden with military personnel from the US, Canada, Lithuania, Poland, Germany, and other countries, according to Bild.
It is designed to connect allied command systems and allow them to exchange data. “The network works in real time. We are moving at high speed,” Canadian Lieutenant Colonel Mike Mendika said.
According to US Army Major Brian Hobek, if Russia attacked a NATO member, information about the attack would reach Wiesbaden and a response could be launched within five minutes.
The system is also intended to automate some of the most routine parts of drone operations. US Army Major Ben Schiff said this could include keeping a drone over a battlefield for long periods while it searches for targets.
The Wiesbaden team is also using 3D printing to develop drones. Schiff said new parts can be produced and tested on the same day, whereas development and testing previously could take months.
NATO believes the system should allow the alliance to adapt to changes on the battlefield faster than an adversary. The project is planned for implementation on a short timeline, as reported by Politico.
On July 7, 2026, NATO launched a new $40 billion initiative called Drone Edge to strengthen the Alliance’s ability to counter unmanned aerial threats.
Announced by Secretary General Mark Rutte during the NATO Defense Industry Forum in Ankara, the five-year program was developed using lessons learned from recent wars, including Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Under the initiative, NATO member states committed to investing in counter-drone technologies, expanding drone pilot training, and increasing the number of drone operators in their armed forces fivefold by the end of 2027.

articles.title: What to Know About the Growing Concerns Over Conditions on the Long-Deployed USS Abraham Lincoln
articles.body:
The USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea in the Middle East for months, and with no clear end in sight for the war in Iran, concerns for those aboard the aircraft carrier—and for the vessel itself—have mounted amid a series of troubling reports.
Another aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, had begun making its way towards the Middle East as of Thursday to replace the Lincoln, multiple news outlets reported. President Donald Trump appeared to confirm the reported ship swap on Friday, saying that the Lincoln "is moving right now, or very shortly and is being replaced with another very similar ship.”
The Washington’s deployment comes as reports have emerged in recent months recounting worsening living conditions, mental health concerns, and supply shortages on board the Lincoln.
Trump seemed to deny the reports on the state of the Lincoln and its crew on Friday, responding “No, they’re not,” in response to a reporter saying that families of the crew members are worried about conditions on board. He also said, when asked if the carrier has been deployed for too long, that it has been deployed “not nearly long enough.”
Defense Secretary Pete Hegeseth on Thursday called the reports of dire conditions on the Lincoln “completely misrepresented.”
“We make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment. Some deployments are longer than others. I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody,” Hegseth, with a hand to his heart, told reporters. “I want them home as soon as everybody else, too.”
The Defense Department did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for comment.
Here’s what to know about the USS Abraham Lincoln, the concerns that have been raised over conditions on board, and the burgeoning calls for its crew to return home.
What is the USS Abraham Lincoln, and how long has it been deployed?
The Lincoln is in its ninth month at sea and has been deployed for more than 260 days.
The vessel works as a mobile airbase and command center with its own defense systems. It’s the length of more than three football fields and has a crew of roughly 5,000 when fully deployed.
It departed from San Diego in November on an alternate deployment, but was redirected towards the Middle East in January to provide tactical support to U.S. forces ahead of the war in Iran, which began with an initial wave of American-Israeli strikes at the end of February.
The Lincoln has played a key defensive role in the war against Iran, having shot down “hundreds and hundreds of missiles” and drone attacks that targeted the vessel, according to Hegseth.
“Every single one of those shots, easily shot down miles and miles away from the Abe Lincoln,” he said in April. “They were blowing ammo into fantasy land.”
The ship has also had a part in enforcing the U.S.’s blockade of Iranian ports.
The Lincoln’s deployment was expected to end in May, but was extended indefinitely.
The reported ship swap with the Washington comes as Trump has reinstated a blockade against Iran in the Strait of Hormuz and peace talks have stalled between the countries.
Reports of issues on board the carrier
Several reports have detailed poor conditions aboard the Lincoln. According to MS Now, which interviewed a dozen family members of crew members, those aboard the ship have been dealing with moldy showers and running out of key toiletries, such as toothpaste, deodorant, and soap. The outlet was also told that crew members are working grueling shifts with limited days off and that there are holes on the Lincoln’s flight deck, where pilots take off and land.
A spouse of a service member on the Lincoln also told CBS News that sailors had previously experienced food shortages. Another report from USA Today contained photos of rationed meals served to crew on board the carrier.
Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, pushed back against reports of food shortages back in April. “In no way, shape or form, has there been a time where in, at least in this deployment, where they’ve not met the nutritional requirements of our menu,” Caudle said.
As the deployment has stretched on and living conditions on board have allegedly deteriorated, the crew of the Lincoln has also reportedly struggled with increasing mental health concerns. The Navy Times and Stars and Stripes reported several instances of crew members on the vessel attempting to jump overboard.
An unnamed U.S. official confirmed to CNN that a crew member went overboard and was rescued last month, an event that was viewed as a mental health incident by the Navy, according to the outlet.
More than 200 families of crew members attended a meeting in San Diego last week with acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao. Many of the families raised a litany of concerns at a later virtual meeting, including about the crew’s mental health, safety, a lack of supplies and food, and water contamination, according to MS Now, which reviewed recordings of the meeting.
Cao was unable to specify during the meeting when the crew on the Lincoln would return home, according to the outlet.
The U.S. military has strongly pushed back against reporting about mental health concerns regarding the Lincoln’s crew.
“We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship,” a U.S. official tells TIME. “Adapting to life at sea can be difficult, so we've learned how to provide resources and help Sailors with these transitions. We are not experiencing an uptick in mental health issues aboard Abraham Lincoln.”
The official says that “religious, medical and mental health professionals” are aboard the Lincoln, including five chaplains, a psychologist, a social worker, three "behavioral health technicians,” and a service dog “to support crew morale and emotional welfare.”
The official did not provide information regarding the ongoing deployment of those aboard the Lincoln “due to operations security.”
“The Sailors and Marines of the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group remain resilient and resolved after more than 260 days at sea, 10,000 aircraft flights, and 1.5 million pounds of ordnance expended,” U.S. Central Command posted on X on Thursday. “No service members aboard the aircraft carrier have died, and the one Sailor who fell overboard Aug. 3 was quickly and safely recovered.”
Democrats push for answers
The reports about conditions on board the Lincoln have sparked calls from several Democrats urging the Defense Department to remedy the situation.
In a letter to Hegseth and Cao, Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, noted that the vessel’s crew members have not been to a port in a record-setting 200-plus days and demanded answers to a series of questions about the crew and the state of the ship.
“There have been widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system,” Blumenthal wrote. “These reports warrant immediate attention, but they also raise a broader question: whether the Navy can sustain the operational tempo now being demanded of its carrier force, particularly as this Administration repeatedly commits U.S. forces to conflicts of its own choosing and increasingly relies on aircraft carriers to sustain those operations.”
He also noted that the long deployment of the Lincoln is not an isolated incident, “suggesting that extended deployments may be becoming a feature rather than an exception of the Navy's force-generation model.” The USS Gerald R. Ford, used for the U.S.’s military operation in Venezuela, spent 326 days at sea before its return in May, Blumenthal wrote, which he noted was “nearly twice the length of a traditional six-month carrier deployment and the longest modern U.S. carrier deployment since the Vietnam era.”
Sen. Ruben Gallego requested an oversight visit to investigate the reports.
“Unlike Donald Trump, I've seen active duty,” Gallego wrote on X. “The way he's treating our service members as he carries out this illegal war is not just disgusting; it’s dangerous. These sailors are owed a sense of when they will go home.”
Gallego referenced the reports of crew members threatening to jump overboard, shifts lasting as long as 16 hours, rationed meals, and moldy showers, which he called “a frightening alarm bell.”
Rep. Sara Jacobs of California, who has introduced a War Powers Resolution to restrict Trump’s authority to continue the conflict in Iran without congressional approval, said that the Lincoln’s crew was “going through hell” and called for an end to the war. She described the reported poor conditions on the carrier as “a personnel issue and a national security risk.”
Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, a Navy veteran, has also taken to social media to call for accountability.
“Our servicemembers deserve better than this,” he said in a video posted to Bluesky. “There needs to be an investigation.” Kelly also blamed Trump having “no way out” of the war with Iran for the extended deployment of those aboard the Lincoln.
Rep. Mike Levin, who represents part of the San Diego region where the Lincoln was deployed from in November, took jabs at Hegseth’s comments downplaying the reports about the carrier.
“When families first raised the alarm back in April, Pete Hegseth called it fake news,” he wrote on X. “These men and women signed up to serve their country. The least their country owes them is hot water, a working toilet, and a real meal. Hegseth cannot even manage that, and he has the nerve to look their families in the eye and call them liars.”
A number of other Democrats have also joined the chorus of concerned voices over the Lincoln, including Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado; Rep. Seth Moulton of Massachusetts; and Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, the top Democrat on the Senate Defense Appropriations subcommittee.

articles.title: South Korea calls for inter-Korean talks to officially end Korean War, halt nuclear advances
articles.body:
Islamuddin Sajid
15 August 2026•Update: 15 August 2026
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Saturday called for direct talks with North Korea to formally end the Korean War and explore practical measures to halt the advancement of Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities, renewing Seoul’s push for peaceful coexistence on the Korean Peninsula, according to local media reports.
Speaking at a ceremony marking the 81st Liberation Day, which commemorates Korea’s liberation from the Japanese 1910-45 colonial rule, Lee urged North Korea to abandon confrontation and begin negotiations, Yonhap News reported.
“Let us put down our intentions to threaten each other and begin discussions to end the long-running war as the directly involved parties,” Lee said, adding: “In the process, (we) may also discuss effective ways to halt the advancement of the North’s nuclear capabilities.”
The Korean War ended in 1953 with an armistice rather than a peace treaty, leaving the two Koreas technically at war.
Lee said his government would seek to replace the “unstable armistice system” with a permanent peace regime, despite Pyongyang’s continued silence toward Seoul’s reconciliation efforts since Lee took office in June last year.
In his Liberation Day speech last year, Lee pledged to respect North Korea's current system and not to pursue unification by absorption or engage in any hostile acts toward the North.
“I hope South and North Korea will sit face-to-face for peaceful coexistence and mutual growth,” Lee said, calling for reduced hostility in perceptions, norms, and systems.
He also proposed a “multilayered security system” to prevent crises, and pledged “preemptive and consistent measures for peace” based on developments on the peninsula.
“By inducing a positive response from the North, I will create a stable Korean Peninsula,” Lee said, adding that peace could strengthen cooperation across Northeast Asia and contribute to a world without nuclear weapons.
On Japan, Lee praised expanded “shuttle diplomacy,” and said Seoul would deepen cooperation with Tokyo in supply chains, energy, and advanced technologies.

articles.title: Polish Defense Ministry annoyed by Zelensky’s manner to ask for Patriot missiles — portal
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 14. /TASS/. Poland is annoyed by the way Vladimir Zelensky is asking Warsaw for missiles for Patriot anti-aircraft missile systems, Wirtualna Polska portal quoted defense sources.
"Zelensky counted Polish missiles for Patriot systems and concluded that [Poland] can afford a large tranche [of missiles]," a Defense Ministry source told the portal. "First of all, we are confused as to how he's so sure about the number of PAC 3 MSE missiles we have in our warehouses. Secondly, it is better to start a discussion on this topic through an official request. Such issues are not resolved through interviews."
According to Defense Ministry Spokesman Janusz Sejmej, the ministry has not yet received an official request from Kiev to transfer missiles for Patriot.
According to the sources, Warsaw is ready to transfer only a small number of such missiles and only as part of a broader NATO tranche.
Besides, Wirtualna Polska said that Kiev may try to exchange the transfer of weapons for new permits to search for the victims of the Volyn massacre. A Foreign Ministry official told the portal that "the history and issues of exhumation [of victims of the Volyn massacre] will not be a subject of bargaining."
According to Wirtualna Polska sources, Zelensky's decision to rebury the remains of one of the leaders of the OUN (Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists, recognized as extremist and banned in Russia) Yevgeny Konovalets from the Netherlands in the Ukrainian capital may dampen Warsaw's desire to transfer to Kiev "expensive and complex weapons systems such as ammunition for Patriot."
Earlier, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that Warsaw would continue to provide Ukraine with military assistance, including missiles for Patriot. According to Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a final decision has not yet been made. In the spring, Poland already transferred several missiles to Patriots under the NATO coalition.

The Ukrainian Armed Forces attacked the Savasleika military airfield in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region, where MiG-31Ks—carriers of Kinzhal aeroballistic missiles—are stationed.
A video of the fire at the airfield was published by the Telegram channel Exilenova+.
The attack on the airfield took place on the morning of August 15. In local chat rooms, residents reported explosions and began asking where exactly the explosion had occurred.
The Savasleika airfield is a Russian military airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region, located approximately 12 km northwest of the city of Kulebaki. The airfield is home to various modifications of the MiG-31 fighter jet, including the MiG-31K, which carries the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal missiles.
This is not the first time the airfield has been targeted. In particular, on August 14, 2024, drones attacked Savasleika. At that time, local sources reported numerous explosions on the airbase grounds.
It later emerged that the strike targeted warehouses and fueling stations on the airfield grounds, around which traces of explosions were observed.

articles.title: 437 civilians dead, 2,610 hurt: the UN says July was the worst month for Ukraine’s civilians in more than four years
articles.body:
437 civilians dead, 2,610 hurt: the UN says July was the worst month for Ukraine’s civilians in more than four years
At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July 2026, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission said in a report.
That was the highest monthly civilian casualty toll since May 2022, when at least 589 civilians were killed and 1,152 others injured.
Separately, the mission said 17 children were killed and 166 injured in July — the highest monthly total of child casualties since April 2022.
Long-range Russian strikes with missiles and drones were the leading cause of civilian deaths and injuries, accounting for 38% of all casualties. Most of these attacks occurred far from the front line, including in major cities.
Short-range drone strikes in front-line areas killed 111 people and injured 710 others — the highest monthly toll since the full-scale war began.
Airstrikes killed 105 civilians and injured 753 in July, a 143% rise in casualties over the previous month.
The UN also recorded a sharp rise in Russian attacks on ships and port infrastructure in the Odesa and Mykolaiv regions, counting at least 39 such attacks in July, including at least 20 strikes on ships. Those attacks killed 19 people and injured 25.
The UN said the attacks are already hurting international shipments of goods and agricultural products through the Black Sea.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Flamingo Missiles Strike Russia’s Soyuz Rocket Factory Behind Its Starlink Rival

Ukraine’s Flamingo Missiles Strike Russia’s Soyuz Rocket Factory Behind Its Starlink Rival
Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles struck the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara overnight on August 15, hitting the factory that produces Soyuz-2 launch vehicles used to deploy Russian military satellites and the Rassvet low-Earth-orbit network—Moscow’s answer to Starlink.
The apparent confirmation that Flamingo cruise missiles were used in the attack came from Fire Point co-founder Denis Shtilerman, who shortly after the strike posted nighttime footage showing the launch of the Ukrainian-made missile.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Samara regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed that a missile strike had hit an industrial facility in the city but did not identify the target. Samara Mayor Ivan Noskov described the attack as a large-scale missile strike.
Local residents reported explosions shortly after a missile alert was issued in the region. Videos published from Samara showed a large fire and a column of smoke rising from an industrial area occupied by the neighboring Progress Rocket Space Centre and Aviakor aircraft plant.
According to Defense Express on August 15, available imagery indicates that the strike may have hit Progress, one of Russia’s key producers of space launch vehicles. The outlet said satellite imagery would still be required to confirm the precise impact point and determine the extent of the damage.
Progress is one of the central enterprises in Russia’s space-launch industry and manufactures the Soyuz-2 family of launch vehicles, including the Soyuz-2.1b.
The Soyuz-2.1b is used to place Russian government and military spacecraft into orbit and has also been used to deploy satellites for Rassvet, a planned Russian low-Earth-orbit communications constellation often described as Moscow’s counterpart to Starlink. On March 23, 2026, a Soyuz-2.1b launched 16 satellites associated with the Rassvet system.
According to Defense Express, the Samara plant represents a particularly concentrated point in Russia’s Soyuz production chain. The enterprise consists of an interconnected industrial complex roughly one kilometer long where launch vehicles pass through successive stages of assembly.
The outlet assessed that the reported strike may have affected the western section of the complex, where later stages of Soyuz production are believed to take place.
Defense Express reported that Russia has conducted approximately six to eight Soyuz-2.1b launches annually since 2022, with the rockets supporting military, government and other space missions.
Soyuz remains one of Russia’s primary methods for placing military satellites into orbit, meaning disruption at Progress could also affect reconnaissance, communications and other space programs beyond Rassvet.
Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy chief of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, previously said Russia was developing the satellite system faster than initially expected. The constellation is intended to provide broadband communications from low Earth orbit and could support both civilian and military users.
The Progress and Aviakor facilities are located roughly 850–950 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border, placing the industrial complex deep inside Russian territory.
Earlier, Russia’s Rassvet satellite network was reported to face a major launch bottleneck because its satellites rely on Soyuz-2.1b rockets produced at the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara. Russia needs at least 18 Soyuz-2.1b launches to deploy the planned 288-satellite constellation, while only six to eight such rockets are typically launched per year.

articles.title: With US-Iran talks stalled, diplomatic efforts expand to unlikely European players
articles.body:
With US-Iran talks stalled, diplomatic efforts expand to unlikely European players
WASHINGTON (AP) — Faced with an increasingly bellicose Iran as talks to end the war have stalled, the Trump administration appears to be reaching out to a broader swath of countries that might be able to help pressure Tehran or ease its hardline position where traditional mediators have not succeeded so far.
While discussions between Iran and Oman, as well as between Iran and Pakistan, Turkey and Qatar, persist at an uneven and unpredictable pace, the U.S. administration quietly has expanded its outreach to include perhaps unlikely interlocutors in Europe.
Just this week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio met in person in Washington with the foreign minister of Austria on Tuesday and held a call with the foreign minister of Greece on Wednesday.
Those interactions were not notable beyond the normal course of relations between the U.S. and two close European allies. The official State Department readouts of the discussions were bland and vague and did not mention Iran by name as a topic of conversation.
But it then emerged that both foreign ministers — almost immediately after their talks with Rubio — spoke Thursday with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The apparent new tack to break the negotiation logjam comes as the U.S. and Iran are both pushing for control of the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial oil shipping corridor. President Donald Trump faces little wiggle room in his next steps as the economic fallout from the war and dwindling stockpiles of key weapons pose political problems for Republicans ahead of November’s midterm congressional elections.
A desperate push is on to break the diplomatic logjam between the US and Iran
The entry by Austria and Greece is likely less of a formal mediation attempt, analysts say, and more reflective of a desperate push to halt the conflict because of the impact it has on an increasing number of countries, beyond those in the Middle East.
“Everyone is just urging both sides to stop this reckless game of chicken,” said Ali Vaez, Iran project director at the International Crisis Group.
It also shows how much Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has forced countries, which otherwise were neutral bystanders to the larger conflict, to exercise any diplomatic sway they may have on their Iranian and American counterparts to kick-start a lasting resolution.
Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, warned that any efforts by Greece, Austria or any other non-mediating country could prove to be futile.
“While the calls to both sides may entail encouraging both Iran and the U.S. back to the negotiating table, such efforts fall short of mediation, which is a very complex endeavor and requires trust to be built by the mediator with both sides,” Yacoubian said.
She added that it’s not something that any country can “just jump into.”
Rubio discussed Iran with his Austrian and Greek counterparts
The State Department said Friday that it could not comment on the timing of calls by other countries’ foreign ministers and maintained that Rubio had made no requests of either to get in touch with Iran or pass messages to Araghchi.
One European diplomat, who was briefed on the matter and spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive diplomatic conversations, said the timing of the calls was not an accident.
The State Department did allow, however, that Iran had been a topic of conversation in Rubio’s discussions, which occurred as Trump is facing serious political headwinds over a war for which he has offered shifting objectives.
No longer purely about making Iran incapable of producing a nuclear weapon, the immediate goal has become reopening the Strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil usually passes through and which was open before the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.
“That’s goal number one: keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country,” Vice President JD Vance said in an interview Thursday on Fox News Channel. But he did not say anything about the strait being open and toll-free for transiting ships, as he had in the past.
The second goal, Vance said, is to ensure that Iran will never get a nuclear weapon.
The two European countries have key connections to the war’s fallout
Austria and Greece may not be obvious choices to assist on the Iran portfolio, but Vienna is home to the International Atomic Energy Agency, which will play a key role in any resolution to the Iran’s nuclear program, and hosted the final negotiations that resulted in the 2015 Iran nuclear deal. Greece is a major maritime nation in the Mediterranean and has significant shipping interests in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
In statements from the Austrian, Greek and Iranian foreign ministries, it was clear that Iran had been a top topic in all of the conversations this week.
The Greek foreign ministry said Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis had been briefed by Araghchi on “regional developments, and in particular on the ongoing talks regarding the Strait of Hormuz.” It said Gerapetritis “underlined the importance of freedom of navigation and maritime security.”
The Austrian foreign ministry offered Austria’s services as a venue for further potential talks with Iran and said Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger had stressed to Araghchi “the urgency of restoring stability in the region through serious diplomatic efforts.”
“There can be no military solution,” it said. “A diplomatic solution remains possible. Our priority is to safeguard freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.”
Iran’s foreign ministry, expectedly, took a different tack in explaining the calls.
It said Friday that in Araghchi’s calls with his European counterparts they discussed “mechanisms for the future management of the Strait of Hormuz,” which he said had been disrupted by the “unlawful aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran.”
In both calls, he accused the U.S. of violating the interim deal signed by both sides in June to end the immediate hostilities and begin broader talks to end the war.
___
Amiri reported from New York. Associated Press writers Derek Gatopolous in Athens and Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland, contributed to this report.

articles.title: DOD Leader Calls for Counter-Drone, Airborne Directed Energy Weapons
articles.body:
A top Pentagon tech official called on industry this week to help the military develop “lighter, more efficient” directed energy weapons designed to go on aircraft and conduct special operations missions or down drones—areas where the Air Force’s directed energy efforts have been quiet as of late.
Directed energy systems such as high-energy lasers and high-power microwave systems are an appealing alternative to expensive munitions for all branches of the U.S. military since they offer deep magazines and can be used near populated areas with a lower risk of collateral damage than high-explosive weapons pose.
Dodd, the assistant secretary of defense for critical technologies, said this promising technology is moving “out of the lab and toward the fight” in an Aug. 12 post on the social media platform X. But there is still critical work to be done, he added.
A key area where the Pentagon needs more from industry is the size and power of these systems: “Smaller. Lighter. More efficient,” Dodd wrote. “Size, weight, and power decide what flies. We want tech on aircraft and high-altitude platforms for counter-drone, expeditionary and special operations missions, and disrupting adversary C2.”
Dodd’s overall message to industry: “Bring us your best. Not slideware—hardware we can put on a range and stress.”
The Air Force has shown a particular interest in directed energy weapons to defend its air bases from drone attacks. Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink told lawmakers in May 20 congressional testimony that the service is “focusing on electronic warfare to directed energy to kinetic capabilities to defend our Airmen and Guardians.”
The Air Force Research Laboratory has worked on high-power microwave technology for years, but the last publicly known test of the Tactical High-power Operational Responder, or THOR, occurred in 2023. The trailer-sized system was “exceptionally effective at disabling” a drone swarm during the demonstration. AFRL announced it was developing a follow-on system to THOR called “Mjolnir,” the name of the hammer wielded by the Norse god Thor.
No tests have been announced since. In its 2027 budget request, the Air Force has requested $91.8 million in research, development, test and evaluation for directed energy technology, with no mention of directed energy in the procurement account. The service projects another $406.6 million in funding between fiscal 2028 and fiscal 3031 to conduct further research on the technology, according to budget documents.
The potential exists for the service to acquire commercially available capabilities including directed-energy tech through the Joint Interagency Task Force 401, according to Air Force officials working on service’s point-defense effort to counter drone attacks.
Besides taking down adversary drones, one of the Air Force’s other major directed energy efforts was the Airborne High Energy Laser, which was planned for the special operations AC-130J gunship. But the AHEL weapon was canceled in 2024 after the program missed its “available integration and flight test window,” Military.com reported.
Besides size and power, Dodd was also critical of the amount of live-fire testing for these critical technologies.
“We need to shoot more, and shoot sooner,” Dodd wrote. “Live fire, in the field, with the units who will actually use these systems — air, land, sea, space. Testing can’t be a once-a-year event on a range. It has to be routine.”
This may be achievable since restrictions on testing directed energy weapons in U.S. airspace have loosened, according to David Bagnati, executive director of JIATF 401.
“We are now accepted to use high-energy lasers in the national airspace,” Bagnati told an audience Aug. 12 at the Space and Missile Defense Symposium in Huntsville, Ala.
Bagnati added that JIATF 401 is now doing “operational assessments at the border. It’s become our operational test bed. We’re also using the southern border as a springboard to bring new capabilities into the national airspace.”
Testing restrictions on directed energy technology in the U.S. eased in April after the Pentagon and the Federal Aviation Administration “completed a thorough safety assessment of a high-energy laser counter-drone system.”
Pentagon and FAA officials agreed to the March assessment after the FAA shut down all flight traffic over El Paso in February in reaction to a U.S. military laser designed for counter-drone operations being fired into the airspace over the U.S.-Mexican border.
Dodd also stressed in his post that the Pentagon needs systems that that combine “every sensor we have and fuse it into one picture.”
“Track and defeat many threats at the same time,” he wrote. “Directed energy has to work alongside kinetic and non-kinetic options, so the operator picks the right effect in seconds.”
Space Editor Courtney Albon contributed to this report.

articles.title: Russia’s MoD threatens to “freeze” Ukrainians this winter, Kyiv responds by saying it will “get warm by the flames of Russian refineries”
articles.body:
On Aug. 14, Russia’s Ministry of Defense published a post on its Telegram channel showing drones with a caption reading: “You’re in for a deep freeze this winter.” The post followed a ministry statement about strikes “on Ukraine’s port infrastructure and seagoing vessels used in the interests of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.”
Several hours later, the AFU’s Center for Strategic Communications responded on its own channel with an image of a burning Russian oil refinery bearing the following caption: “We’ll warm ourselves with the flames of Russian refineries.”
Earlier today, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said it was unacceptable to halt the fighting along the current line of contact:
“This is not just about how comfortably someone lives today. Our people are suffering, people are dying from these terrorist acts. It is about our responsibility for the thousand-year history of the Russian state.”
Lavrov said Russia would intensify its actions against Ukraine.
“We are already doing this,” he said. “They are already starting to groan.”
The previous day, Aug. 13, Reuters reported that Ukraine had sent Russia a proposal through a third party to mutually halt attacks on civilian sites in the Black Sea, saying the fighting in the region had threatened global food supply chains. Several days earlier, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Ankara had sent Kyiv and Moscow proposals to create a moratorium mechanism on strikes against commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
“Russia has not received a formal Turkish appeal through official channels specifying the terms of this initiative,” Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova responded on Aug. 14.
In June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky published an open letter to Vladimir Putin proposing a direct meeting between the two and a ceasefire along the entire front line for the duration of the talks. But no such developments ever materialized.
Since 2022, Russia has been intensifying its strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure every fall in an effort to leave the country without electricity and heating during the winter months. In fall 2024, Russia managed to disable about 80% of Ukraine’s power generating capacity, damaging nearly all the country’s major thermal power plants. Ahead of the upcoming winter, Russian forces have focused on destroying the infrastructure of Ukraine’s electricity grid, targeting substations and power lines in the Sumy, Chernihiv, and Kharkiv regions.

articles.title: Trump says record-setting Navy deployment to support Iran operations ‘not nearly long enough’
articles.body:
Trump says USS Lincoln’s record time at sea during Iran operations ‘not nearly long enough’
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday downplayed the toll on American sailors enduring nearly nine months at sea on the USS Abraham Lincoln as concerns escalated about mental health and supply issues aboard the aircraft carrier supporting U.S. operations against Iran.
In a brief exchange with reporters before flying to New York for an event to highlight falling violent crime rates across the U.S., Trump refuted that family members have raised concerns about the deployment’s length and even said that the deployment — which includes a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days — is “not nearly long enough.”
“That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it’s being replaced with another very similar ship,” Trump said when asked about the lengthy deployment. The acting navy secretary, Hung Cao, said the Lincoln “will return home soon” in a social media post on Friday.
Trump strode into office for a second term vowing to avoid lengthy and expensive military entanglements. And after launching the Iran war, alongside Israel, Trump and his advisers said the conflict would last a matter of weeks. The war is now more than five months old.
But on Friday, during his crime address in Garden City, New York, he acknowledged that he’s used the U.S. military “a little bit more than I wanted to,” while asserting anew that the U.S. operation against Iran is going well. He even said, seemingly in jest, that “pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.”
“I’ll never apologize,” Trump added about the war and its impact on oil prices. “I did the right thing.”
Democrats demand Pentagon briefing on USS Lincoln
Extended deployments of carriers during the Iran conflict have raised concerns about the impact on service members who are away from home for long periods as well as the increasing strain on the ships and their equipment.
Several Democratic lawmakers, including Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ruben Gallego of Arizona, are pressing for accountability from the Pentagon over conditions aboard the Lincoln, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday said were “completely misrepresented.”
Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., who served three tours in Iraq and Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division and 75th Ranger Regiment before being elected, took to social media to criticize Trump’s comments, saying on X that “President Trump does not care about our servicemembers or their families.”
Top Democrats on the House Oversight Committee have requested a classified briefing on the ship’s food inventory, sanitation issues and healthcare availability, as well as an assessment of how much longer it would be deployed before relief arrives.
Republicans have been less outspoken about the situation on the Lincoln. The GOP chairmen of the House and Senate armed services committees did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
While hostilities between the U.S. and Iran have calmed in recent weeks, the Navy has reimposed a blockade on Iranian ports in the crucial Strait of Hormuz, and the Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war. Hegseth said the U.S. military can maintain the blockage of Iranian ports “indefinitely.”
Another aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, left port in Da Nang, Vietnam, last week, and is expected to replace the USS Lincoln, one of two aircraft carriers currently deployed in the Middle East.
After reports emerged that sailors on the Lincoln are struggling with mental health concerns, the Navy said it has “not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship,” though officials have declined to provide data, citing operational security and patient privacy concerns.
A Navy official said a sailor aboard the Lincoln went overboard in early August but the person was quickly recovered, treated by the ship’s medical department and transferred off ship for follow-on care. The official would not say whether it was being considered a suicide attempt.
U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, has also pushed back on reports about poor conditions.
___
AP writers Collin Binkley in Garden City, New York, and Michelle L. Price and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump says US will hit Iran hard economically after Bessent issues warning
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said Friday that he would soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory, following a Truth Social post on Wednesday in which he said of the waterway, "I think we will keep it."
"Pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," Trump told a crowd at a Garden City, New York, event honoring police.
Trump said the declaration would come "after we [the US] finish defeating Iran," which he described as being "very badly defeated."
He described the US naval blockade in the strait as "unstoppable" and a "wall of steel," saying, "No ships get through unless we want them to."
Trump added that he "built [up]" the US military, which he said he used "a little more than I wanted to, frankly, but that's okay."
"We cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he emphasized. "Do we agree? Can't let them."
The US president described Iran as a "very evil country" and the "number one state sponsor of terrorism in the world."
"Remember that when you have to pay a little bit more [for gasoline]," Trump added.
Trump: Operation Midnight Hammer prevented Iranian nuclear weapons
Trump credited the US military's Operation Midnight Hammer for preventing Tehran from acquiring such weapons.
"If we didn't hit them, you would have had a nuclear weapon," he said, noting it as an outcome that would have been a "very sad day for this country and the entire world."
Trump's comments came a day after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the US would impose measures on Tehran that have "never been seen" as soon as next week.
Iran responds, says the regime does not fear threats
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi responded to Trump's comments in an X/Twitter post later on Friday, saying that the Strait of Hormuz "cannot be seized by tweet, nor by aircraft carrier, nor by issuing an order, nor by an election speech."
"Iran neither fears threats nor cowers before displays of power," Gharibabadi added.
On Saturday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iranian news outlet Shahrara News that while Iran has decided not to resume talks with the US, separate talks with Oman were focused on defining a sea route through the Strait of Hormuz.
Araghchi reiterated previous assertions from Tehran that the US would have to meet specific conditions for shipping to resume through the waterway.
He added that messages being exchanged with Washington via Qatar and Pakistan do not amount to negotiations.
Reuters and Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

articles.title: First warehouses burned, now payment system is down: Ukraine launches dual campaign against Russia’s largest marketplace that reportedly moves drone parts
articles.body:
Ukraine has hit Russia's biggest marketplace in cyberspace as well as with drones. Cyber specialists disrupted Wildberries' operations across Russia, Ukraine's Defense Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) reports.
Ukraine says that Wildberries is not ordinary commerce but a piece of Russia's war logistics. According to the military command, the network moves military-related goods, and President Zelenskyy has said Russia uses the platform to bring in sanctioned drone components, which is why Ukraine has spent weeks burning its warehouses and now strikes its servers.
HUR reports that on 10 and 11 August, specialists from the Cyber Corps community attacked Wildberries' digital infrastructure, causing failures in its payment and customer service systems.
The attack hit payments and support
The disruption struck where customers feel it. Because of the problems with the payment infrastructure, users complained they could not complete certain transactions.
For a platform whose whole value is the frictionless movement of goods and money, a payment system that will not process transactions is a direct hit to the business.
The strain spread to customer service. At the same time, the load on the support service rose, causing failures in the contact centers, so the attack degraded both the ability to pay and the ability to get help across Russia.
It pairs with the warehouse strikes
In July, Ukrainian drones destroyed eight Wildberries warehouses, about 15.4% of the marketplace's storage.
Pairing strikes on physical infrastructure with Ukrainian cyber operations strengthens the pressure on the company, HUR assessed.
The logic is to squeeze the same target from two directions at once: burn the warehouses that store the goods, then disable the systems that move them to customers, so damage in one domain amplifies damage in the other.
Earlier, Ukraine hit the Progress Rocket Space Center in Samara, which builds Soyuz-2 rockets used to launch Rassvet, Russia’s planned alternative to Starlink.

articles.title: Russia plans to remove border zones separating Russia from occupied Ukrainian territories
articles.body:
Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) plans to abolish special border zones along several boundaries with Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia, according to draft orders reviewed by the Russian outlet Agentstvo.
The proposed changes would remove restrictions that currently treat movement between Russia and occupied parts of Ukraine much like crossing an international border. The FSB says the move follows Russia’s claimed incorporation of the occupied Ukrainian territories into Russia.
FSB seeks to remove border zones
The draft orders, as reported by Ukrainska Pravda, would invalidate previous FSB orders establishing border zones along the boundaries between Russia’s Rostov and Voronezh oblasts and the occupied territories of Ukraine.
A similar change is planned for occupied Crimea, where the current border zone along the boundary with occupied Kherson Oblast would be abolished.
The existing rules effectively impose additional controls on people entering and leaving the occupied territories, making movement subject to procedures similar to those used at Russia’s state border.
In the draft orders, the FSB justifies the changes by referring to the alleged “admission into the Russian Federation” of the occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, and Kherson oblasts.
Russia illegally claimed to annex those territories, along with Zaporizhzhia Oblast, in September 2022. The move has been rejected by Ukraine and the international community, and Russia does not control all of the territory it claims to have annexed.
Border zone would remain around Crimea's islands
The FSB proposal would not completely eliminate the border zone in occupied Crimea.
A restricted zone would remain “within the boundaries of the Black Sea islands belonging to the Russian Federation,” according to the draft. The FSB’s regional directorate would determine where and when people could enter the zone and would install warning signs.
The proposed changes would remove the existing border zones along Russia’s boundaries with occupied Ukrainian territories, while retaining a border zone around certain Black Sea islands in occupied Crimea.
Russia treats occupied territory as part of its territory
The planned changes reflect Moscow’s effort to incorporate occupied Ukrainian territories into Russia’s administrative and legal system.
In September 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed so-called “accession treaties” claiming to incorporate Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts into Russia. Russia’s parliament subsequently approved the claims.
The treaties purported to define the boundaries of the annexed territories according to the borders they had on the day Russia claimed to admit them into the Russian Federation, despite Russia not controlling the entirety of those regions.
Russia previously used similar measures to formalize its control over occupied Crimea after illegally annexing the peninsula in 2014.

articles.title: ‘We can no longer move towards small dreams’: Modi’s message to India on Independence Day (VIDEO)

‘We can no longer move towards small dreams’: Modi’s message to India on Independence Day (VIDEO)
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday outlined the country’s achievements and priorities for future growth as the world’s largest democracy marked its 80th Independence Day.
Addressing the nation after hoisting the Indian national flag at Delhi’s iconic Red Fort, Modi cited India’s rapid economic growth from being one of the ‘Fragile Five’ economies in 2013 to a $4.15 trillion, fast-growing major economy, and said the country is emerging in the eyes of the world as a widely accepted and respected nation.
The ‘Fragile Five’, was a term for Türkiye, Brazil, India, South Africa, and Indonesia, which were overly dependent on unpredictable foreign investments and large current account deficits to fuel their economic growth.
“Our country is not going to move forward with small dreams,” Modi said, noting the country rises through the “strength of its dreams, its resolutions, and its capabilities.”
📹🇮🇳 ‘We Can No Longer Move Forward With Small Dreams’: Modi’s Big Message From Red Fort
The prime minister urged Indians to “dream big,” saying a nation rises through the strength of its dreams, resolve and capabilities. https://t.co/F71jMC9sPTpic.twitter.com/GgzxMjxJmL
Fuel for growth
Listing India’s achievements in the last 12 years since his Bharatiya Janata Party came to power, Modi said the country’s defense production has increased fourfold, electronic manufacturing has increased sevenfold, and digital transactions have increased 100 times.
Modi pointed to the success of his Make-in-India initiative, and cited the three chip plants that the country has built, with plans to add eight more. “Chips are indispensable; without them, the world would come to a standstill,” he said, as Indian positions itself to benefit from the global demand for chips driven by the boom in artificial intelligence and data centers.
This, however, raises the demands for energy security, Modi acknowledged, stating that the South Asian nation will need electricity “on a very large scale.”
The Indian leader reiterated the country’s target of achieving a capacity of 100 GW of nuclear power by 2047 and highlighted the need for accelerating offshore exploration to find oil and gas that could replace imported energy that makes the national economy vulnerable to external shocks.
⚛️ AI Needs Power, PM Modi Wants Nuclear To Bring It
Pointing to GPUs, AI and data centres, Modi said, “Energy security is the need of our times,” adding that India will need electricity “on a very large scale” and is targeting 100 GW of nuclear power by 2047.
The SHANTI Act,… https://t.co/dIK8Pogw5hpic.twitter.com/Ihr51lv9xx
New Delhi in December 2025 passed the SHANTI Act (the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India Act), which modernizes India’s nuclear framework and opens the door to greater private sector participation in India’s nuclear energy industry, which has been lacking so far.
The country currently operates 24 nuclear power reactors across seven different sites with a total installed capacity of 8.78 GW. This includes Russia-built Kudankulam designed to house six VVER-1000 reactors with a total planned capacity of 6,000 MW. Units 1 and 2 were connected to the national grid in 2013 and 2016, respectively, while units 3, 4, 5, and 6 are at different stages of implementation and construction.
Overall, India currently has ten reactor units with a combined capacity of 8,000 MW are under construction, while pre-project activities for ten additional reactors are also underway.
Focus on self-relaence
“It is our conviction that India must not be dependent on other countries. We must become self-reliant,” Modi stated, calling for strengthening the country’s capabilities and protecting national interests.
Modi outlined seven broad areas that he said would be central to his government’s goal of turning India into a developed country by 2047. These included manufacturing, agriculture and food production, technology and innovation, connectivity – including high-speed rail – defense production, the green and blue economy – such as green hydrogen, renewables and energy storage – as well as the expansion of India’s soft power such as yoga, which he called “an energy for the world, and a major source of confidence for India.”
“India possesses a stable political mandate, a stable government, a vibrant democracy, a robust judiciary, and guiding all of us is the Constitution of India,” Modi said. He also noted that the youth are the “biggest beneficiaries” of India’s development, and said his government will run free online coaching networks for competitive exams for students. The move comes weeks after student-led unrest rocked the country’s capital and led to the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
Celebrating friendship
India achieved independence from British rule on August 15, 1947, through largely non-violent means and beginning the end of Western colonial rule over the world. Independence Day celebrations were held across the country, in state capitals and various offices.
In Moscow, Indian Ambassador Vinay Kumar raised the tricolor at the Indian Embassy as the Indian national anthem was sung. In a symbolic move, a group of Russian and Indian motorcyclists rode across the city to celebrate the decades of close ties, marked by cooperation and trust.

Long live the friendship of Russia-India,” Alipov added.

articles.title: Far-right troops bid farewell to Nazi collaborator with torch-lit march in Kiev (VIDEO)
