Far-right troops bid farewell to Nazi collaborator with torch-lit march in Kiev (VIDEO)
Servicemen belonging to a far-right Ukrainian military unit have held a torch-lit farewell ceremony in Kiev for Evgeny Konovalets, the founder of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), which collaborated with Nazi Germany.
Konovalets’ remains were exhumed at a cemetery in the city of Rotterdam in the Netherlands earlier this week and delivered to Ukraine on Wednesday. They will be temporarily reburied at the National Military Memorial Cemetery outside the capital.
After dark, fighters of the 3rd Army Corps staged a farewell ceremony for the Nazi collaborator at a cathedral in central Kiev.
The unit was formed earlier this year by members of the Azov nationalist movement, which stems from the neo-Nazi Azov regiment that emerged in 2014 during Kiev’s crackdown on Donbass. The regiment faced repeated accusations of war crimes, including torture, rape, and looting, from the UN and international NGOs such as Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International.
Велике повернення великого Провідника: полковник Євген Коновалець — на рідній землі!
Минулої ночі через майже 90 років на цвинтарі Кросвейк у Роттердамі засновник ОУН та командир Січових Стрільців, полковник Євген Коновалець, повернувся до України.
На почесну варту до… pic.twitter.com/gwGBqqedlz
The coffin with Konovalets’ remains was driven to the cathedral in a historic Austin armored vehicle from the period of the Russian Civil War of 1917-1922. It was greeted at the scene by two rows of troops, holding torches in their hands.
The unit’s commander Andrey ‘White Leader’ Biletsky hailed Konovalets and claimed that the current generation of Ukrainian fighters should accomplish the objectives he fought for.
Konovalets fought the Soviet Union during the Russian Civil War as a colonel in the army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic, and led the OUN from its founding in 1929 until he was killed by Soviet agent Pavel Sudoplatov in Rotterdam in 1938. According to declassified documents, a group of Ukrainian nationalists that he led – codenamed ‘Consul I’ – supplied German intelligence with data on Poland from 1925 and moved into “espionage and sabotage” work inside the Soviet Union after 1939.
The reburial of Konovalets is part of a push by Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to build a “Pantheon of outstanding Ukrainians,” which he says will fulfill a “moral duty” to bring home those who “defended the idea of independence.” Kiev has already reburied several Nazi-linked figures, including another OUN leader, Andrey Melnik, in May.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova previously blasted efforts to reinter Konovalets, accusing Zelensky of “dancing on the bones” of those who fell victim to the OUN and once again confirming the “misanthropic essence” of his government.
While Moscow has long condemned Kiev for glorification of Nazi collaborators, Zelensky’s campaign also triggered a diplomatic rupture between Ukraine and Poland. The dispute erupted after he decided to name a special forces unit ‘Heroes of the UPA’, in honor of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which killed more than 100,000 Poles during the 1943–1945 Volhynia massacres.

articles.title: ‘Food Truck One,’ expandable decoys, and the propaganda ruin

‘Food Truck One,’ expandable decoys, and the propaganda ruin
TEHRAN — The official narrative survived for a month. It portrayed an American president boarding Air Force One on July 8 following a NATO summit in Ankara, waving to the cameras, and flying west. The reality was far more humiliating.
Donald Trump boarded the Boeing 747 purely for the cameras. Minutes later, he cowardly slipped out a door on the opposite side of the aircraft and stepped into a raised airport catering container. The truck lowered him to the tarmac and drove him to a waiting military C-32A.
The 747 departed Ankara as a decoy. It carried Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House aides, and the traveling press pool. Journalists were ordered to keep their window shades closed. None of them knew the president was already gone.
The White House justified this massive deception by citing a threat of a shoulder-fired missile. Yet the intelligence did not come from American spies. It came from Israel.
‘Israeli-derived’ and ‘low-confidence’
Washington launched an elaborate security ruse on the soil of a NATO ally based on intelligence that its own analysts doubted. One U.S. official described the threat reports plainly: “Israeli-derived, not U.S.-generated, and viewed as low confidence.”
The CIA found the intelligence uncompelling. Turkish intelligence services reportedly investigated and found no corroborating evidence.
Reuters noted the Ankara extraction “underscores how Israeli intelligence is influencing the Trump administration’s decision-making about Iran.”
Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen questioned whether the Israeli material could stand on its own, saying, “I am very curious about the extent to which the Israeli-provided intelligence was not only credible but independently verifiable.” Van Hollen added, “This all seems a little fantastical.”
The decoy flight and the human shields
If the older Air Force One was genuinely too dangerous for the “commander in chief,” the administration decided it was perfectly acceptable for senior Cabinet members and journalists to absorb the supposed risk.
Rubio and Bessent occupy the fourth and fifth spots in the presidential line of succession. They were left on the alleged target aircraft.
The ethical vacuum of using unaware civilians and staff as human shields provoked immediate disgust. A White House reporter, speaking anonymously to Times of India, stated the principle clearly: “Reporters take risks as part of the job, but not on behalf of the president.”
Steven Cash, a former CIA intelligence officer, delivered an even blunter verdict. “It appears that the idea was we can reduce the danger to President Trump by offering up 100 or so people to be killed by the Iranians in his place,” Cash said.
Trump offered little sympathy for the passengers. He claimed the C-32A he flew on was “at greater risk” because attackers would logically target his actual plane.
When asked about the journalists forced to fly blind with their shades drawn, he replied, “Probably on a dangerous flight... But if I go, you go. Right?” He later mused, “Perhaps someday you want to change professions.”
This casual disregard fractured usual partisan defenses. The influential podcaster Joe Rogan, who has supported Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign, highlighted the moral failure. “Those press people were signing up for something they didn’t know,” Rogan said. “That’s crazy. When you want to know, like, who’s more important, you or the president, that’s when you find out.”
Senator Richard Blumenthal demanded answers, calling the operation “unprecedented and surreal” and “downright scary.” He asked, “What precautions were taken to make sure that all of the passengers on that Air Force One … were safe?”
The White House response, delivered by Communications Director Steven Cheung, offered only broad justifications. “There are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,” Cheung said.
History shows a different way. When President Bill Clinton used a decoy plane in Pakistan in 2000, the press was briefed.
Susan Page, the White House Correspondents’ Association president at the time, recalled the transparency. “They told me about the extraordinary security procedures being taken,” Page said. The Trump administration discarded that precedent entirely.
The propaganda ruin
The political wreckage of the Ankara escape extends far beyond Washington. A government that speaks relentlessly of American dominance watched its president hide in a catering crate to escape regional airspace.
Social media users leveraged the imagery instantly. The extraction vehicle was dubbed “Food Truck One.”
Cartoons and AI-generated pictures depicted the president hiding among French fries and Diet Cokes. The ridicule crossed oceans.
Iran’s embassy in South Africa posted a meme of the incident on X, predicting the American president “will be hidden in a trash can before long.”
The mockery works because it targets the core vulnerability of the administration’s narrative. Trump declared the war on Iran won months ago. Yet the Strait of Hormuz still works based on Iranian arrangements, U.S. missile interceptor stocks are heavily depleted, and the commander in chief cannot safely leave a NATO capital.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer linked the tarmac panic directly to the faltering war effort. “It is unacceptable that Congress was kept in the dark and instead learned about this serious threat through press reports,” Schumer said. “Trump has put America’s sons and daughters in harm’s way by getting into an unnecessary and reckless war.”
Illinois governor and presidential hopeful billionaire J.B. Pritzker echoed the sentiment, focusing on the character revealed by the escape. “He put people in harm’s way to save himself,” Pritzker said. “He slinked away literally in a catering truck while the reporters and his own staff were on a plane that apparently was under threat.”
Trump has continued to project indifference. “I guess there was a threat out there,” he told reporters. “I didn’t really ask too much about it... I don’t worry about anything, to be honest.”
The footage from the Ankara tarmac tells a different story. The war Trump escalated has generated consequences that now dictate his physical movements.
The American empire projected absolute military supremacy. It ended the night with its leader pathetically concealed among the meal trays, fleeing a threat its own spies barely believed existed.

articles.title: Flamingo missiles reportedly strike an industrial site beside a factory building rockets for Russia’s Starlink rival
articles.body:
Samara Oblast Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev confirmed that a missile struck an unnamed industrial enterprise overnight on 15 August 2026. Andrii Kovalenko, head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, said the Progress Rocket Space Center was burning. He provided no damage details.
Progress would be a significant target because it builds Soyuz-2 rockets used to launch Rassvet, Russia’s planned alternative to Starlink. Its Soyuz-2.1b rockets carried Russia’s first serial-production Rassvet satellites into orbit this year. However, neither the governor’s statement nor available imagery establishes that Progress itself was hit.
Exilenova+ published early footage from Samara and reported that a Flamingo cruise missile had struck the city.
A mature Rassvet network could reduce Russia’s dependence on unauthorized Starlink terminals. For now, neither damage to Progress nor the reported use of a Flamingo missile has been independently confirmed.
Open-source analysts at Falcon Insight Map geolocated the smoke near Aviakor’s Building No. 106. Militarnyi said Aviakor and Progress sit a few hundred meters apart, and available images could not establish which enterprise was hit. The industrial area lies roughly 900 kilometers from Ukraine.
Kyiv pushes strikes deeper into Russia
Ukraine has increasingly attacked factories far behind the front to disrupt the supply chains sustaining Russian weapons production.
Speaking separately to Euromaidan Press, defense scholar Marc DeVore urged Ukraine to disrupt Russian missile production and launches. Retired US Lieutenant General Ben Hodges noted that Ukraine’s interceptor shortage means it is better to “kill the archer” than try to stop every arrow.
In June 2026, Ukrainian cruise missiles hit a Voronezh semiconductor plant supplying components for the Pantsir-S1, Iskander-K, and Kh-101.
A reported Flamingo strike in July also damaged the Avitek defense plant in Kirov, more than 1,200 kilometers from Ukraine.
The deeper strikes come as Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) says Russian factories are producing 110% to 120% of their monthly missile quotas.
How the Samara plant supports Russia’s Starlink alternative
The Progress factory in Samara makes the Soyuz-2.1b rockets used to launch Rassvet satellites developed by Russia’s Bureau 1440. A second batch of 16 entered orbit in July, bringing the serial constellation to 32.
Rassvet’s coverage remains intermittent. However, Moscow plans to deploy 292 satellites by the end of 2027 and 924 by 2035. A Ukrainian defense adviser estimated that continuous service would require 200–250 satellites.

articles.title: Inside Russia’s new gulag: what The New Yorker found in a Rostov cell of Ukrainian women
articles.body:
Inside Russia’s new gulag: what The New Yorker found in a Rostov cell of Ukrainian women
Since 2014 — and especially since 2022 — Russia has seized and still holds at least 1,878 Ukrainian civilians. These are only the confirmed cases; the real number is likely far higher. At least 223 of them are women. Like Ukrainian prisoners of war, many civilian hostages from Ukraine have been tortured and are held in inhumane conditions. But unlike military prisoners, they have little hope of going free in an exchange. Ukraine, citing the Geneva Conventions, insists they should never have been detained at all. Russia points to rulings from its own courts and says they are serving sentences for terrorism, treason, and other serious crimes. The two sides do not trade military prisoners for civilians, which leaves the return of these detainees unresolved.
The New Yorker has published a long piece about Ukrainian women who ended up sharing a cell at Rostov pretrial detention center No. 1. For the story, the magazine’s Joshua Yaffa spoke with former inmates and exchanged letters with several of the women still held there. Some had served in Ukraine’s armed forces; others had no ties to the military. The first group has been exchanged; the second is still in custody. Meduza retells the stories of two of them.
Warning: This article contains descriptions of torture.
Valentina Zayarnaya, 66
Zayarnaya taught English in Amvrosiivka, a small city near Donetsk. Two months into the full-scale war, she got a call from an old acquaintance, a former Ukrainian border guard whom she knew only as Dima. They had met in 2018 at the Hnutove crossing, on the de facto border between the self-proclaimed Donetsk People’s Republic (“DNR”) and the Ukrainian-controlled parts of the Donetsk region. They struck up a conversation, exchanged phone numbers, and stayed in regular touch over the following years. Zayarnaya had once lost a child she had wanted to name Dima, and she came to think of this second Dima not simply as an acquaintance but as family.
Dima was not his real name. The man who introduced himself to Zayarnaya that way is Denys Storozhuk. At the start of the full-scale war, his border-guard unit was sent to defend Mariupol. Storozhuk spent three weeks hidden in a utility shaft deep inside the Azovstal plant, then made it out of the city and called Zayarnaya. When she told him she had gotten her son Kostya out of the embattled city, Storozhuk asked her to get him out, too. He lied, telling her he had taken no part in the war. She drove down the very next day and brought him from Mariupol to Amvrosiivka. They got lucky at the checkpoints: no one searched the car or asked for their documents.
Storozhuk lived with Zayarnaya for nearly a year. One day, he asked her to pick up a package for him at an address in Donetsk. Inside was a forged passport that would have let him leave occupied territory. When she arrived, FSB officers were waiting and quickly arrested her. Under questioning, Zayarnaya learned the truth about him: He was a lieutenant colonel in the Ukrainian military and had fought at Azovstal, escaping before Ukrainian forces surrendered. He had also stayed in touch with fellow servicemen, and investigators said he had hidden weapons and explosives at her house. Zayarnaya was accused of helping Storozhuk plan an assassination attempt on a “DNR” lawmaker and was sentenced to 12 years. Storozhuk was detained as well, but he was exchanged in the fall of 2024, before the trial; he was later sentenced in absentia to 22 years.
Zayarnaya’s cellmates were frustrated that Storozhuk had concealed his identity. But by their account, she always defended him — even though, during the investigation, FSB officers had beaten her son and threatened to send him to a mental hospital unless she gave them the testimony they wanted. She signed a confession, then tried to kill herself.
In a letter to The New Yorker, Zayarnaya called Storozhuk a second son and wrote: “The most important thing is that my boys are alive and free.” She said she considers prison “a school of survival, a test of the humanity and decency in each of us.” In custody, she has gone on teaching English — now to her cellmates.
Natalia Vlasova, 44
Vlasova has been in detention for more than seven years. In court, she said it all began in 2018, when an acquaintance who worked for the SBU, Ukraine’s security service, asked her to go to Donetsk and fill in for Serhii Hruzinov, an agent working at a chandelier shop who needed to travel to Kyiv. Vlasova agreed because, in return, she was promised help with a criminal drug-possession case against her. Soon after that trip came another: this time, she was asked to check whether Hruzinov had switched sides. She was detained trying to enter the “DNR” on a forged passport.
Vlasova was taken to Izolyatsia, a former insulation-materials plant in Donetsk that was turned into a secret prison in 2014. There, she was tortured for months. Her captors stripped her, bound her with tape, and shocked her with electricity. A doctor was present at many of these sessions; when she lost consciousness, he revived her by shoving a cotton ball doused in ammonia up her nose, and the torture started again. She said that one of her torturers was Vasily Yevdokimov, an official in the “DNR” state security ministry who is believed to have created Izolyatsia. “He personally filed my teeth with a metal file, twisted my nipples, and tried to force a bottle into my vagina,” Vlasova said in court.
A person who heard her testimony told The New Yorker that when Vlasova finished describing the torture, a judge asked whether she wanted to enter her written notes into the court record. “We were in shock,” that person said. The judge’s reaction seemed to be a quiet signal: “It was a gesture on the scale he was allowed.” But despite the gesture — and despite the fact that Vlasova recanted her earlier statements in court, saying they had been extracted under torture — she was sentenced to 18 years. Her conviction included the attempted assassination of Yevdokimov, the man she said had tortured her.
Over her seven years in custody, Vlasova has watched countless times as other women were freed and she was left behind. At the Rostov detention center, she kept a bag of clean clothes at the ready, in case she, too, was one day told, “Pack your things — you’re leaving.” So far, that has not happened.
Her daughter, Yulia, who lives with her father in Kyiv, is now 11. Her father and other relatives tried to keep Yulia from seeing news of her mother’s torture, but within days of the testimony she had read the coverage. She had only one question, The New Yorker reported: “What are nipples?” Last year, Yulia took part in a rally in Kyiv’s Independence Square to call attention to Ukrainian women held prisoner in Russia. She brought a sign that referred to one of her last memories of her mother: “Mom, remember you promised me a kitten?”

articles.title: Russian agent accused of directing strikes on Nikopol detained in Dnipropetrovsk region
articles.body:
Russian agent accused of directing strikes on Nikopol detained in Dnipropetrovsk region
The SBU said this in a statement seen by Ukrinform.
"According to the investigation, the spotter was a local man who had been recruited by the enemy and deserted from a Ukrainian Armed Forces training center before taking the oath. While hiding at his home, the suspect began looking for 'easy' ways to make money through Telegram channels. A Russian intelligence officer contacted him in one of the thematic groups and offered him cooperation," the statement said.
In exchange for the promise of "quick" earnings, the agent began monitoring the positions of Ukrainian Defense Forces in the frontline city.
"The enemy's priority targets included reserve command posts and combat positions of Ukrainian air defense units protecting the airspace over the Dnipropetrovsk region. The suspect was documented moving around the area to secretly photograph and mark on Google Maps facilities that he believed were being used by Ukrainian defenders," the SBU said.
Counterintelligence officers exposed the suspect at an early stage of his espionage activities and detained him at a private residence.
At the same time, measures were taken to secure Ukrainian military positions and troop movement routes.
During a search, investigators seized a mobile phone containing evidence of the suspect's cooperation with Russian military intelligence.
SBU investigators notified him that he was suspected of high treason under Part 2 of Article 111 of Ukraine's Criminal Code, committed under martial law.
The suspect has been remanded in custody without the right to post bail. He faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.

articles.title: Vladislav Balgrabsky surrendered to save five soldiers under his command. Now Russia is putting him on trial for treason.
articles.body:
Vladislav Balgrabsky surrendered to save five soldiers under his command. Now Russia is putting him on trial for treason.
The criminal case against Vladislav Balgrabsky, a 30-year-old who fought in the war, has reached the 2nd Western District Military Court, the independent Russian outlet Mediazona reported. He is charged with voluntarily surrendering to the enemy, desertion, and treason.
In April 2025, Ukrainian journalist Yuriy Butusov published a video of Balgrabsky in which the Russian officer said he had signed a contract with Russia’s Defense Ministry in the summer of 2024 and had served as a company commander in the 7th Motorized Rifle Regiment.
Balgrabsky said he surrendered to Ukrainian forces along with five soldiers after receiving an order that was clearly impossible to carry out. “I decided to surrender in order to survive, to be able to see my family, my child. I’ll just stay alive and keep the guys alive. […] These people trusted me, and they survived,” he said in the video. At the end of the video, he called on other Russian servicemen to surrender as well.
The video drew more than 990,000 views. Eight months after it appeared, in December 2025, a case card showing that Balgrabsky’s detention had been extended was posted on the website of the Moscow Garrison Military Court. His detention was extended twice more after that. According to Mediazona, this usually means that a person is in custody and that their case is being heard in person rather than in absentia.
Balgrabsky appears to have been returned to Russia in a prisoner exchange sometime between April and December 2025 — a period in which Russia and Ukraine carried out at least seven such exchanges.
The article criminalizing voluntary surrender was added to Russia’s Criminal Code in 2022, after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the mobilization campaign. Russia’s Supreme Court has said that a surrender counts as voluntary when a person surrenders knowingly and has the ability to put up “decisive resistance.”
The first conviction under the statute came in April 2025, when Junior Sergeant Roman Ivanishin received a 15-year sentence in a penal colony. He had surrendered to Ukrainian forces in 2023 and appeared in a video urging other Russian servicemen to flee their units. He was later returned to Russia in a prisoner exchange.

articles.title: The True Story Behind The Brink of War
articles.body:
The Reykjavik Summit—when U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet Union President Mikhail Gorbachev talked in person in 1986—is not known as an iconic bit of American history. But the face-to-face conversation between the leaders, held over Oct. 11 and 12 in the Icelandic capital, proved to be an important step toward the end of the Cold War.
The summit (or meeting, depending on who you ask) came after “an unexpected invitation from Gorbachev,” says Pete Souza, the former Presidential photographer for Reagan. At the time the Reagan administration refused to call it a summit.
“Before two leaders like that have a summit meeting, there's lots of prep work that goes into it,” recalls Souza. “But this was very last minute. The Reagan administration went to great effort leading up to Reykjavik, to not call it a summit. They’d say, ‘It’s just a meeting, and we’re not characterizing it as a summit.’”
The summit’s purpose was to discuss the arms controls between the two nations, in hopes of bringing an end to the long-lasting threat of nuclear war hanging over both countries, and the world as a whole. Over 30 hours, Reagan and Gorbachev fiercely debated in an effort to bring peace and the end of the Cold War. Now, a new film from writer-director Michael Russell Gunn, The Brink of War, gives this historical moment a worthy spotlight. The film stars Jeff Daniels as Reagan, Jared Harris as Gorbachev, and J.K. Simmons as Secretary of State George Shultz.
For Gunn, the idea for The Brink of War came from a meeting he had with the real George Shultz, to whom the film is dedicated. Shultz told him all about the Reykjavik Summit. “I had never heard of this summit before,” says Gunn, “but once I found out I couldn’t stop thinking of it.”
There was one particular detail from their conversation that made Gunn realize the Reykjavik Summit was a pivotal moment in world history. “Schultz told me he asked Gorbachev years later—and I included this in the movie—what changed to bring an end to the Cold War,” says Gunn. “Gorbachev responded with one word: ‘Reykjavik.’” From that moment, Gunn knew he had a movie.
Shultz detailed a memory to Gunn about how he’d stand outside the meeting room when Gorbachev and Reagan went in, and these two military officers would be standing there, each of them holding a nuclear football. “If things had gone badly, Reagan and Gorbachev could walk out, press the buttons, and end it all,” says Gunn. “The idea of these two military officers with all the power in the world literally in their hands, was an extraordinary memory to share, and an extraordinary thing for us to film.”
Gunn was struck by how generous Shultz was with his time, and he gave the filmmaker something that would allow for an exceptionally realistic approach: the declassified transcripts of the meeting. The transcripts allowed Gunn another first-hand account of the summit, as well as the opportunity to lift dialogue directly from the real conversations into the script. A number of conversations are nearly verbatim to what the transcripts show, though Gunn admits to finessing certain moments for cinematic purposes. “I tried to make it as close as I possibly could,” says Gunn.
The only points Gunn really departed from the transcripts were things they didn’t reveal. “I didn’t have transcripts of what was going on with the advisors, or what was happening with the first ladies,” he says. For that, he researched several books, pointing to Dutch: A Memoir of Ronald Reagan by Edmund Morris and Gorbachev by Willaim Taubman to help gather a fuller sense of the people surrounding the leaders.
Gunn calls himself a lifelong fan of Souza’s photography, and he pulled the original proofs from Souza’s summit photography at the National Security Archives. On a whim, he cold emailed Souza to see if he was available to join them on the film shoot to produce the film’s still photography. To Gunn’s delight, Souza accepted. The veteran photographer provided Gunn great assistance in faithfully recreating the summit, and the photos Souza took have a striking resemblance to the original photos from ‘86.
The summit itself was an incredibly tense showdown that occurred over a brief 30 hours. The discussions of arms controls with a view to bring an end to the Cold War came tantalizingly close to fruition. At one point during the summit, Reagan and Gorbachev were close to agreeing on a deal that would remove every single nuclear missile from the planet, a moment in the transcript that Gunn was particularly stunned by. “Gorbachev proposed eliminating all these different classes of weapons that the Americans weren’t expecting,” recalls Souza. “There was a moment when Reagan and his team thought ‘This can be historic.’ There was a real excitement about it.”
That excitement was all too brief. As a condition of eliminating these weapons, Gorbachev demanded an end to the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), nicknamed “Star Wars,” a missile defense system proposed to protect the United States from attack. “The whole SDI thing doomed that hope. Gorbachev wanted Reagan to not go any further with the SDI. That was the sticking point, and the mood changed to disappointment,” says Souza.
“My main takeaway of President Reagan behind the scenes was he had such an even keeled disposition,” says Souza. “It would take so much to get him angry or pissed off. One of the few times where he got pissed off was at the end of Reykjavik.”
The summit was considered a failure at the time, with no agreement struck at the end. However, it ultimately provided a breakthrough between Reagan and Gorbachev. The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty was signed on December 8, 1987, which was an enormous step forward to the end of the Cold War, which ultimately concluded with the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. If it wasn’t for the Reykjavik summit, it’s likely that treaty never would have been signed.
Gunn hopes the film can show audiences that if we work with people who disagree with us, we can forge a better future.
“For one, I want the audience to walk out of the cinema with hope. That as divided as we are, it's been worse,” Gunn says. “We were literally about to blow up the world with enemies, and we found a way out of that. The second thing I want people to walk out with is courage. It takes courage to engage with people you disagree with. We've decided that listening means we agree, and that's not true.”
Adds Gunn: “They didn't agree, but they listened to one another, and they found a way to make a better, safer world.”

articles.title: Ukraine: 18 of 26 Russian oil and stolen-grain ships face no sanctions
articles.body:
On 14 August, Ukraine's Military Intelligence (HUR) published data on 26 vessels via its War&Sanctions portal, noting that 18 ships face no sanctions from any of Ukraine's partner countries.
The agency said the ships carry Russian oil, liquefied natural gas (LNG), or agricultural products from occupied Ukraine. Euromaidan Press could not independently verify HUR’s vessel records.
Russia relies on maritime trade both to fund its war through energy exports and to sell crops taken from occupied Ukraine. Kyiv began building a dedicated system against Russia’s shadow grain fleet in April, modeled on its oil-fleet campaign. A US bill introduced this week would also target vessels, owners, insurers, and ports involved in sanctions evasion. HUR’s new list shows how many ships remain outside those restrictions.
Russia’s grain shadow fleet
HUR divided the 26 vessels into three groups:
- oil tankers serving Lukoil, Rosneft, Surgutneftegas, Novatek, Tatneft, and Gazprom;
- dry-cargo ships using the occupied ports of Berdiansk, Sevastopol, Kerch, and Feodosia;
- LNG carriers moving gas from the sanctioned SAAM FSU floating storage unit, which holds LNG from the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project.
HUR highlighted three of the 18 vessels that are not facing partner sanctions. The bulk carrier LAMAR S repeatedly loaded wheat at the Avlita terminal in occupied Sevastopol in 2026 for delivery abroad, including to Syria, the agency said.
NAYA FALCON carried baking soda and granulated wheat bran from occupied Sevastopol to Egypt and Cyprus, HUR said. The agency linked the oil tanker GREGAL to UAE-based Cymare Navigation FZC, which it described as affiliated with Sovcomflot, Russia’s state-controlled shipping company.
Russia steals grain while striking Ukraine’s exports
Crops taken from occupied land are sold abroad as Russian produce, while Russia's attacks leave Ukraine’s legitimate harvest with fewer routes to market.
Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service said Russia sold more than 2 million tons of grain from occupied Ukraine as Russian produce in 2025. The agency said ship-to-ship transfers at Kavkaz helped conceal its origin.
Meanwhile, Russian attacks have squeezed Ukraine’s legitimate grain trade. Strikes on civilian ships brought the Black Sea corridor to a near standstill during the July harvest peak. Ten people died when Russian missiles hit the grain-laden Golden Leo on 19 July.
HUR called on Ukraine and its partners to synchronize sanctions and detain vessels that violate restrictions. It said the measures could curb Russia’s maritime logistics and war funding.

articles.title: Captured Akhmat fighter says he chose Ukraine and a drone guided him away from Russia’s ranks
articles.body:
A former fighter from the Akhmat forces, armed formations loyal to Chechnya’s Kremlin-backed ruler Ramzan Kadyrov, said he wants to fight for Ukraine after nearly a year in captivity.
Identified only as Magomed, he gave his account to Dmytro Karpenko, a Ukrainian journalist and blogger known for interviewing Russian prisoners of war, in a video published on 9 August 2026. Militarnyi, a Ukrainian military news outlet, reported on the interview on 13 August.
Magomed’s reported crossing reflects a divide that has placed Chechen fighters on both sides of Russia’s war. Since 2014, Kadyrov-loyal formations have fought for Moscow, while anti-Kremlin Chechens seeking independence from Russia have supported Kyiv.
Magomed’s account traces one fighter’s claimed passage from the first camp toward the second after Russians allegedly killed his brother. His account has not been independently verified.
The Chechen fighter said he had served near Svitlodarsk, Bakhmut, and Horlivka, including evacuating soldiers’ bodies.
Magomed also claimed two Chechens had crossed before him, prompting Russian commanders to check fighters’ phones and tighten surveillance.
According to Magomed, he later followed a Ukrainian drone toward Ukrainian positions with other Chechens. Ukrainian troops dropped medicine, water, and a radio to guide them. A Russian FPV drone attacked during the crossing and killed one Chechen, he alleged.
Ukrainian forces received the survivors and handed Magomed to the police brigade "Liut". His captivity began on 29 August 2025. Magomed also alleged that Russians killed his brother and called the death an epileptic seizure. Magomed said that drove him to fight Russia.
Militarnyi reported that Magomed had joined the International Legion, which is run by Ukraine's military intelligence. However, Karpenko’s video description says he wants to join the legion. Neither source explained the discrepancy.
What is Akhmat?
Akhmat, the unit Magomed belonged to, provides Russia with frontline troops and rear-area security. UK intelligence estimated in 2024 that around 9,000 personnel served in pro-Russian Chechen units in Ukraine.
Kadyrov’s reach has also expanded during the war. A later investigation found that his armed network had grown to 20 units across Russia’s military and security structures.
The Akhmat group's influence may extend beyond military operations. In January 2026, ATESH, a Ukrainian-Crimean Tatar partisan group, said Moscow planned to hand occupied Mariupol to Akhmat as a reward for Chechen leaders’ loyalty. The resistance organization claimed that arriving Chechen forces sought control of the city’s resources and industry.
Chechens also fight for Ukraine
On the other side, Chechens seeking an independent Ichkeria (the indigenous Chechen name for Chechnya) have fought for Ukraine since 2014.
In April 2026, Ukrainian intelligence said Shamanbat, a Ukrainian special unit that includes Free Ichkeria fighters, helped conduct drone and artillery strikes on Akhmat positions. The agency claimed the operation killed dozens of Akhmat personnel and wounded about 80.
